Title: Roman Ramble & Woodland Walk
Summary:
Join OutdoorLads for a lovely late-summer circular hike in the Hampshire/Berkshire borders exploring the remarkably well-preserved ruins of the Roman town of Calleva Atrebatum, followed by a walk through the beautiful woodland of Benyon's Inclosure and Hundred Acre Piece, part of the Englefield Estate.
The sights
Calleva Atrebatum
Prior to the Roman conquest in 43 AD, Calleva Atrebatum was the Iron Age capital of the Atrebates tribe. After 50 AD, the Romans turned this settlement into a major town which served as a regional administrative centre. The town was laid out in a traditional grid pattern with a forum at its heart, and with roads radiating out to other towns such as Londinium (London) & Venta Belgarum (Winchester). At its peak in the 3rd & 4th centuries, the town had a population of nearly 10,000 and covered around 100 acres. The massive walls were built initially as earth embankments around 200, then in masonry around 270 to protect against Saxon raids in the south of England. Following the Roman withdrawal in 410, Calleva was abandoned after 450, and became one of a small minority of major Roman towns not to develop into a modern settlement.
Due to its abandonment, the remains of the town and the walls were undisturbed until excavations began in 1866, and continue to this day, under the auspices of Reading University. Calleva is now owned by Hampshire County Council & managed by English Heritage, and open to the public.
The Englefield Estate
This 14,000 acre rural estate in West Berkshire & North Hampshire has belonged to the Benyon family for hundreds of years. At its heart is Englefield House near Theale, but we'll be walking through the beautiful woodland of the Hampshire section, comprising Benyon's Inclosure & Hundred Acre Piece. The estate welcomes responsible walkers, and there is an extensive network of permissive paths to use in addition to public footpaths.
The route
From Mortimer station, we'll head south-west for about an hour to cross into Hampshire and reach Calleva Atrebatum. We'll pause to visit the amphitheatre & Silchester church before walking on top of the Roman walls to the south gate, where we will descend and continue outside the walls to the west gate. From here, we'll walk to Silchester village where we will stop for lunch on the green, and those that wish can have a quick drink in the Calleva Arms PH. After lunch, we'll head north to reach and pass through Benyon's Inclosure and Hundred Acre Piece. Returning to Berkshire, the final stretch skirts around the northern edge of Mortimer village to return to the station.

Summary:
Our route follows the winding Wear in places, and old railway lines in others. We pass a number of disused pits that have now been turned into a park and a nature reserve. There are stretches that are more suburban, and some roadside walking, but I have tried to keep this to a minimum. This walk starts at
Finchale Priory

Lumley Castle
(sadly not home to Joanna!).  We skirt parts of the golf course, before getting a better view after passing through Lumley Thicks (woodlands).
We then follow a shaded path towards Bournmoor, and on to
Elba Park
, where you can see an interesting sculpture commemorating the Wooden Wagonway. We pass close to Fence Houses, before continuing on to the
Rainton Meadows Nature Reserve
.
We walk on and pass Leamside, before we take a short loop through Cocken Woods and reconnect with the River Wear, back to our starting point.
After the walk, there will be an opportunity for a drink at The Three Horseshoes, before we head home.

We’ll finish with a short amble through the park, taking in views of the Abbey from different angles before returning to the visitor area. There’ll be time at the end for an optional trip to a nearby café for anyone who fancies rounding off the walk with something warm and restorative.

Summary:

The course is 5k long, run entirely on paved paths. Some sections of the course may accumulate mud, leaves and puddles after rain.
The course starts on The Cliff, opposite The Green and goes north along the promenade towards Hartlepool Marina and Maritime Way, on to the skeleton pier and turns at 1.82 miles (2.95km) which is just after the first set of steps on the right.

Title: Cnicht and the Moelwyns
Summary:
Summiting a trio of Eryri's Moelwynion, this 14km / 8.7 mile circular mountain walk will give us wonderful views of Bae Tremadog (Tremdoc Bay) and a close up look of a slate miners' settlement above Blaenau Ffestiniog.
Starting in the village of Croesor we will pick up the Cambrian Way heading north east steadily but steeply gaining height to summit the dagger-like Cnicht (689m). Descending the opposite flank we'll head deeper towards the core of the Moelwynion range before cutting south and east in search of the miner's cottages above the Cwmorthin Quarry.
Continuing on the Cambrian Way up through huge mounds of slate and passing the open mine entrances we'll head south and west to steadily ascend again up to Moelwyn Mawr (770m) giving a glorious view out over Bae Tremadog in the west.
Dropping down to just under 600m, leaving the Cambrian Way and hopping quickly up to circle and summit the last of our Moelwynion trio, Moelwyn Bach (710m), we shall steadily descend towards the setting sun in the west then the last stretch of road north back to the car park.

Redpoint Birmingham Climbing Centre
Indoor climbing centres offer the challenges of climbing that you'll find on natural rock crags - simply indoors! It's a fun way to stay fit, make new friends & develop your climbing skills.
Climbing
- Unlike Indoor Bouldering there is a certain amount of skill to be mastered, such as tying in knots & belaying a partner, as well as the climbs being higher than in bouldering. If you are new to climbing or would like a refresher, then this is just for you!! If you’ve climbed before, can safely tie into a harness & can competently belay, then there’s plenty of choices of top-rope & lead climbing on offer here.
Bouldering

The bouldering rooms are just as interesting as its climbing routes, over 200 bouldering problems have been organised into graded circuits to provide something for everyone.

Title: Derby Bouldering - MONDAY - Beginners Welcome
Summary:
Swap trainers for climbing shoes and join OutdoorLads for an evening of INDOOR BOULDERING at Derby’s Climbing Unit
NOTE: If you are climbing with us for the first time
, either as an experienced climber or beginner, please send a note to the
Event Leader
telling them about your experience and goals. There is a limit to the number of beginners that we can accommodate at each session. Each beginner needs to be supervised so we need to ensure there are enough experienced climbers to help you out. Climbing is great fun! It's a fab workout, in a social environment, and anyone can do it! Give it a go!
What is Bouldering?
It's a form of climbing where instead of long high routes, the 'problems' tend to be shorter and focus on technique, balance, body positioning and sometimes power. Because of this different emphasis, bouldering doesn't have the hassle of climbing with ropes, harnesses and belaying, which makes it an excellent activity for newcomers to the sport. No wonder it's often regarded as the 'purest' form of climbing.
If you're a seasoned climber you won't need convincing about the benefits of bouldering, but for those who've never climbed more than a staircase, the benefits are wide ranging: from the physical - improved strength, tone, balance, power and coordination; mental - problem solving, focus, concentration and body awareness; to the emotional - relaxation, a sense of achievement and a feeling that mind and body are working together perfectly ('feeling psyched'). On top of all this, bouldering tends to be a very social sport where you can hang out with mates and each have a go as you feel regardless of what level you climb at.
I'm new to Bouldering - can I come along?
If you have never tried bouldering before it is recommended that you have a guided session from the event leader, who will go through everything you will need to know to boulder safely before joining in with the rest of the group.
I've been Bouldering before?
As above, everyone attending the event  must abide by the centre's T&Cs etc. As an experienced boulderer you are responsible for your own safety, actions and involvement at all times. As such, you should use your own judgement in taking up advice given either by OutdoorLads Volunteers or other experienced climbers.

Title: An Arkengarthdale Adventure
Summary:
Our
7 mile (11.2KM)
walk takes in some of the finest Yorkshire Dales countryside.
We will explore a picturesque and fairly quiet valley once famous for its lead mining. Walking through fields, pastures and woodland we will have time to stop and admire the classic Swaledale meadow landscapes with its many field barns (Coo Uses) used to house cattle and hay when they weren't routinely brought down to the farm in the winter.
The walk takes us along Arkengarthdale, following Arkle Beck to Arkle Town, before crossing the river and walking back towards Reeth. There will be ample opportunity to appreciate the diverse nature of this narrow valley, its landscapes and it's wildlife we will encounter along the way. There are fantastic views of Fremington Edge, and Calver Hill on either side of the valley.
The area of Calver Hill has been inhabited since the Mesolithic period, when the nomadic population of this country were hunter/gatherers and this area was a rich source of food. Evidence of them being in this area include arrow heads and flint tools dating back over 6000BP. Fremington Edge reminds us of the valuable lead mining industry that took place along the valley during the 18th and 19th Century.
We can finally round off our day with a drink in one of the hostelries in Reeth village centre

Title: Following giants on Ilkla Moor Baht 'at
Summary:

We'll begin from Ilkley, taking a circuitous route along the tarn to the
Cow and Calf rocks
. According to legend, the giant Rombald split the Calf from the Cow while fleeing an enemy. His angry wife, dropped the stones from her skirt to form the Skirtful of Stones you'll see.
From here we'll join the Dales Way link to
the Twelve Apostles
- the remains of a Bronze age stone circle. Next we'll visit other sites including the Thimble stones, Cowper's Cross, and the Badger Stones before wending our way to White Wells on the outcrop above Ilkley before descending back to town.
There’ll be an optional trip to a café at the end of the walk.

Title: Hull Social October 2026
Summary:
Join us as we return to one of the National Geographic "Top 10 places to visit in 2026"
Hull is rich in culture, with stunning museums; art galleries; cream phone boxes; Europe's largest 'submarium' (complete with Sharks); old bars that played host to the beginning of the English Civil War and the backdrop for many TV and film productions (Victoria, The Crown, A Royal Night out, Enola Holmes).  The city also has a buzzing gay scene in the newest Freedom Quarter, which hosts multiple gay bars and clubs.

We’ll discover more about Hull’s fascinating maritime history, its fishing industry and marina, as well as enjoying the impressive collection of artworks at Ferens Art Gallery, which has exhibitions spread across both floors.

Title: A Big Bridge, Windmills, Wetlands and a Walkabout.
Summary:
This is on of a series of events taking place in Hull over the weekend. Take a look at the
Hull Social page
to see what else is going on.
Come along for an exploration walk over the impressive Humber Bridge, once the world’s longest single-span suspension bridge, taking in the spectacular views across the Humber Estuary.
This is a pleasant walk, mostly on the level. Starting at Hessle Whiting Mill, we’ll cross the bridge before following paths along the Humber through the eastern parts of the Barton and Barrow Clay Pits. These former industrial sites have now been transformed into a series of water pools, nature reserves and important wild-bird breeding sites.
We’ll then leave the pits via one of the old boatyards and cross the fields towards the town of Barton-upon-Humber, where there will be some time to explore the town or relax in a café or pub.
From Barton, we’ll make our way back across the Humber Bridge, giving us a second opportunity to enjoy the impressive estuary views as we return to East Yorkshire.
The route is approximately 10 miles.
Dogs:
We’ll be passing through areas of nature reserve, so dogs must be kept under control and on a lead when near wild birds. There is also a short section along minor roads where there is no footpath.

Title: To have and to hold - Bingley Little Theatre
Summary:
Step out of the everyday and into a night of humour and heartfelt drama as we swap muddy boots for the theatre and settle in for a production of ‘To have and to hold’ brought to life by Bingley Little Theatre.
A warm blend of Northern grit and real heart that tackles memory, ageing and all things family with a smile and a laugh. Anyone who has watched their own parents grow older will find something and someone to recognise here.
After sixty years of marriage, settled into their Yorkshire retirement village, Jack and Florence have turned bickering into an art form. They are getting along just fine, with the support of their cousin and the hilarious interventions from their friend the locals know as ‘Rhubarb Eddie’….but will their anxious son, bouncing between London and LA, and their snobby daughter, eyeing a move to Australia, leave them to live out their days in peace?

Title: Hart, Butts and Beach
Summary:
Total distance: about 18 km (approx. 11.2 miles), with 190 m (625 feet) of ascent. Approximately 5.5 hours, including lunch. This walk includes farmland, quiet country lanes, woodlands, and some beach walking.
We walk along quiet country lanes for the beginning of this walk, including the amusingly named Butts Lane. There are views towards the North Sea.
We pass through Bellows Burn before continuing our path through farmland, past a large farmhouse, on our way to Monk Hesleden. Here, we join the Hart-to-Haswell Walkway. This section of the walk has plenty of shade.
Towards the end of the path, we cross the railway track and head towards Crimdon Beach and the
Dunes Café
. There will be time to stop for those who wish to purchase refreshments. As the seating is for customers' use only, those who bring their own packed lunch can head down to the beach to eat. Those using the cafe can rejoin the rest of the group there after their meal.
As the tide will be low, there is then a decent stretch of the walk along the beach itself to
Steetley Pier
. This industrial relic, built to supply water to a local magnesite plant, now provides a home to many seabirds and is interesting to photograph.
We loop back on ourselves and complete the final section of Hart-to-Haswell Walkway, before beginning a gradual ascent back towards our starting point. We cross farmland with several gates, and in places, various animals (horses, sheep, longhorn cattle).
For those who may like a drink after, the best local option is
the Raby Arms
in Hart, under 1/2 mile away.
And for all who also like to run, there’s the option to take part in Hartlepool parkrun with other OutdoorLads before this walk - just sign up on
that event page
.
Dogs: Well-behaved, under control dogs are welcome at this event.
Dogs should be kept on a lead whenever signposted, whenever we are in the vicinity of livestock, and at the event leader's request. Many stretches of this walk include sheep roaming. I would also note that there are a few up-and-over wall stiles towards the end of the walk, so you get a bit of an upper-body workout lifting your dogs over them. You'll need to make sure you're carrying sufficient extra water for your four-legged friend. We do not encounter much natural water on this walk. If you're unsure, contact the leader for guidance.

Title: Pendle Hill Halloween Walk
Summary:
On Halloween itself, the hill made famous by witchcraft, mist and mystery will cast its spell over the Ribble Valley and the Borough of Pendle on this atmospheric high-level circular walk. 💀
Halloween costumes are optional—but very welcome!  🎃
We’ll tackle the whaleback shape of Lancashire’s Pendle Hill from Barley, travelling via Newchurch-in-Pendle, home of the Demdike family of Pendle Witch fame. 🧙🏻‍♀️
From there, we’ll pass Fell Wood, overlooking the Ogden Reservoirs, before climbing through Ogden Clough and onto the Pendle Hill plateau.
We’ll follow the plateau clockwise along its north-western flanks, taking in sweeping views across the Ribble Valley and towards the Yorkshire Dales, before reaching the trig point at Big End. 🧟‍♂️
We’ll then descend through the farms of Pendle Side and Windy Harbour, pass Lower Black Moss Reservoir and return to Barley for a well-earned pint—
the perfect ending to a Halloween adventure
. 👻
Pictures - Copyright Johnny Williams

Title: Historical Trefil and the Charterist Caves
Summary:
A varied and interesting route taking in a range of historical and culturally important locations against the backdrop of stunning views of the Bannau Brycheiniog.
Starting in Trefil -  at 409m the highest village in Wales - we follow the old Bryn Oer tram road north past the limestone quarries of the area. After a slight detour to the Duke's Table, we head to the other worldly abandoned North Quarry. This strange landscape is a favoured filming location and has appeared on many TV series and films, including Dr Who, Torchwood, Wrath of the Titans, Merlin and the Hitch Hiker’s Guide to the Galaxy. Here we will visit the curios Naughty Stone and take in the views down Duffryn Crawnon and across the Bannau Brycheiniog - described as one of the most beautiful views in Wales. This area was a favourite place of Aneurin 'Nye' Bevan - a former coal miner in the area, he became Minister of Health and spearheaded the creation of the National Health Service in 1948. He loved to roam in these hills and his ashes are scattered on this unique landscape.
We head back through the woods before heading across to Mynydd Llangynidr. Here we will be off the path and crossing open moorland taking in more sweeping views as we climb Garn Fach and then onto Garn Fawr - a large bronze age burial Cairn. From here we navigate across to Ogof Fawr  - more commonly known as Charterist Caves. We will gather at the mouth of the caves to learn about its role in the Charterist Uprising of 1839 and its role in modern British democracy. After we descend across a limestone landscape back to the eerie disused western quarry before heading back to the village for optional refreshments in the
Quarrymen's Arms
pub.
This is a great walk to get a feel of the wilderness of the Bannau Brycheiniog without committing to a long day in the hills, while learning how local communities have worked, lived and been inspired by the landscape.
All pictures by
David Pugh
/
Caerphilly Adventure Group
and used with permission.
Difficulty & Distance: 14km walk and 300m of ascent in mixed terrain, with some climbing and crossing of open exposed moorland. Parts also pass through old quarries and limestone landscapes with uneven surfaces.

Title: Bannau Brycheiniog - the Fforest Fawr Fan Clwb
Summary:
Fforest Fawr is a UNESCO Global Geopark is set within the Bannau Brycheiniog National Park in south Wales. It sits to the West of the more famous central Beacons - it is less popular but no less dramatic than its neighbours. The peaks may not be as high but the views are just as spectacular, the routes as challenging and it benefits from being far quieter. The wild mountains and hidden valleys of the geopark are the result of nearly 500 million years of Earth history. This fascinating area contains evidence of ancient seas, mountain building and sea level and climate change scattered across a landscape that was shaped by the last ice age.
Parking at the quieter Craig Cerrig-gleisiad parking area we start by exploring this often overlooked Nature Reserve. It is a dramatic glacial cwm,  often nicknamed the "Eiger of the Beacons" for its steep, imposing north-facing cliffs. It is a haven for rare arctic-alpine plants and upland birds. We climb around the area to the peak of Fan Frynych (629) to take in the views across the whole Bannau Brycheiniog range. We then traverse across the top of the cliffs before crossing wild moorland to climb Fan Fawr (734) to take in views across to Corn Du and Pen y Fan  We descend down towards Storey Arms. Depending on conditions and time we will either heading back to the reserve via  Craig y Fro or along the Taff Trail.  This is a tough walk in places - the ascent and descent of Fan Fawr can be steep and the area can feel more remote and isolated than its busier neighbours. However we start gently with a good warm up on Fran Frynach and we are rewarded with experiencing the quiet wilderness of this special area.
There are excellent opportunities to try out your navigation skills on this walk - whatever your level. If you are interested in learning or practising any techniques on the day let me know beforehand.
All pictures by
David Pugh
/
Caerphilly Adventure Group
and used with permission.
Difficulty & Distance: 14km, 650m ascent on some rough ground and moorland on mountain upland

Title: Machen and Ruperra Loop
Summary:
This walk mixes woodland, historic villages and old castles and provides sweeping views across the Rhymney Valley and towards the coast, just 10 mins off the M4 between Cardiff and Newport
Starting from Machen Village Hall we will follow part of the popular Forge trail into Coed Cefn-pwll-du, which hosts a popular (and challenging) weekly Park Trail Run. Here we will deviate from the original Forge trail and pick up the Cambrian way and head into the Llwyn Hir woods and head to Draethen and up to the Ruperra Hill Fort and view point. This boasts commanding views over to Cardiff, Newport, the Gwent levels and the Channel. Here we will take a breather and admire the sweeping views across to Newport, Cardiff and beyond. This old fort sits in the land adjacent to Caerphilly's "other" castle - no less impressive than its bigger town centre counterpart it has a colourful past and controversial future  From here we will cut across farmland and an old iron bridge to Lower Machen with its historic church. We then climb the slopes of Mynydd Machen via Royal Oak, where we are rewarded with more views across the Rhymney Valley.
This route is a moderate walk on good paths. It is just under 16km in length and there is approx 650m of ascent and steep sections. If the weather is bad or we decide our legs aren't in it the route can be cut short to miss out Mynydd Machen, reducing the distance to 11km and 350m ascent.
All pictures by
David Pugh
/
Caerphilly Adventure Group
and used with permission.
Difficulty & Distance: 16km in length and approx 650m of ascent on mixed terrain. Some steep short climbs.

Title: Rugged and Romantic: the 'Lads, the Mens and some Studs
Summary:
The 'rugged and romantic' of the title applies (apart from to us and any strapping strangers we might meet) to the landscape which is some of the most hidden and hilly in West Sussex. Although possessing a topography unlike the sweeping South Downs, the area is part of that national park. The 'Lads' in the title might be obvious, but 'The Mens' is a wooded nature reserve with an untamed, uncanny feeling, its ancient trees soaring then falling and their hulks becoming a home to a myriad fungi. The area's remoteness includes from the masses, as its sturdy sandstone, tiled and timber-framed buildings house both the upper crust and their horses (the studs of the title) in equal luxury.
The sights:
The Mens:
The Sussex Wildlife Trust
website
says: 'A largely unex­plored wood, it certainly has an untamed, mysterious feeling to it and many people describe it as ‘wild’...A lack of management in recent years has added to this silvicultural diversity. As you start to wander through the reserve, you will begin to orientate yourself – there are old tracks and banks separating woodland compartments and heavily incised streams full of bryophytes that fracture and divide the site – old fallen giants are found everywhere, many...now home to important populations of saproxylic inverte­brates, fungi (almost 600 species found so far) and bats. Trees are almost always left as they have fallen and the amazing structure this creates adds to the wild feel.' The name is from the Anglo-Saxon ‘ge-mænnes’, meaning common land.
Crimbourne Farm:
A big half H-shaped house, rambling thanks to the accretions of many centuries from the C16 to the C19. Good barns all around in stone, tile and weatherboarding. Stables and stud farm adjacent. Set in one of the most picturesque landscapes in the county.
Stopham:
Just a simple church and a few cottages with superb countryside all around. St Mary's is C11 and C12 with a fine collection of memorial brasses to the local Bartelot family in the floor. Stopham Manor is a splendid stone farmhouse of the C16. Stopham Bridge from 1483 occupies an idyllic spot despite the new bridge being built almost alongside. The centre arch was raised in 1822.
Bedham:
Just a farm, a derelict Victorian chapel and school and some fine houses set high on a wooded sandstone ridge in some of the hilliest and most remote scenery in Sussex. The chapel was founded in 1880, and abandoned in 1959.
Dogs:
I love having dogs on my walks and this one is well-suited to them as there are few fields of livestock. However, there will be some stiles and roads to cross. A dog off a lead must be obedient.
The
route
(click the link to see it at the Ordnance Survey website):
We'll get to Coombelands Lane using an alleyway then use it to go north past Pickhurst, where we'll pick up a bridleway to go to Pallingham Quay, heading west. We'll then use Horsebridge Hill to go north and northeast before turning west along Crimbourne Lane. We'll then turn south and follow the Serpent Trail across The Mens and Hammonds Wood to Bedham where we'll have lunch. At Bedham Lane we'll turn southeast and at Mockbeggars turn down a bridleway to Harwoods Green. There, we'll use Woodcote Lane to get to Stopham. Leaving Stopham, we'll walk beside the A283 on the footpath, cross old Stopham Bridge, go to the pub, then follow the Wey South Path heading northeast back to Coombelands Lane and the alleyway back to the station.

Title: Rossendale Ramble to Hog Lowe Pike and Tor Hill
Summary:
Join Johnny and OutdoorLads for a 14.3km walk following the Rossendale Way up on the moorland above Rossendale and Haslingden taking in Hog Lowe Pike (382m) and the flat-top Tor Hill (340m).
From our start point, we’ll head north and pick up the Rossendale Way skirting the base of Oswaldtwislte Moor, before heading south, crossing the Grane Road and heading up to Edgerton Moss before reaching the highest point on today’s walk, Hog Lowe Pike which offers commanding views over towards Darwen Moor, Jubilee Tower and Winter Hill.
We’ll then head south east to Causeway Height, before heading down and picking up the Rossendale Way again and following around the secluded Musbury Valley. We’ll then begin our short ascent up on to the iconic flat-top Tor Hill, which offers fantastic views over Haslingden.
From here, we’ll then descend back into the end of Musbury Valley, before a short steep ascent to skirt the side of Musbury Heights and Ogden Reservoir before heading over Calf Hey dam and back to the car park where we start for a well earned coffee and cake.

Title: Reading Indoor Bouldering
Summary:
This bouldering session presents an ideal opportunity for a fun evening of what I call sociable workout where we take on a wide range of physical (and in fact mental) challenges with the atmosphere always friendly and cheerful. All levels are welcome!
The beauty of bouldering lies in its simplicity: you don't need ropes or a harness, just some climbing shoes which can be hired at the centre and a drive to get the top and overcome some trepidation. It's also a fundamentally social experience, with most of the session spent discussing how to solve particular climbing routes, aka problems, or catching up with each other in between climbs. Bouldering is a great way to get into climbing, come and see what all the fuss is about!
All skill levels are welcome
. If you're new to climbing, we've got you covered with tailored guidance, boosting your skills and confidence while ensuring your safety on and around the wall. Don’t worry about needing to invest in gear before you try. The Climbing Hangar offers
free shoe rentals
so you don’t have to shell out for shoes until you know bouldering is for you.
Experienced boulderer? Dive in and embrace the challenges independently. Just remember to follow the centre's rules for your own safety.
Our ethos is inclusivity. I keep our group tight-knit to foster connection and ensure personalised coaching for everyone, regardless of your experience level. Many climbers started their journeys relatively “late” in life, incl. some session leaders
🤫
We convene at the
Climbing Hangar in Reading
, one of the largest climbing centres in the region. The generously spacious and friendly cafe/lounge is my personal favourite where you can find us socialising, having a cuppa, snacks or even pizza before and after the climbs.
If you have never climbed at the Climbing Hangar in Reading before, you must book an induction slot:
https://www.theclimbinghangar.com/locations/reading

complete the waiver form that is linked in the confirmation email
once you've booked an induction slot.

Title: Londinium, Lundenburh, Londres - London from the Romans to the Normans
Summary:
Over 1000 years separate the oldest feature on this walk (the Roman amphitheatre of 70 AD) from the most recent we'll survey (St Bartholomew's Church of 1123), and although we won't see two key sights as they charge for entry (the Tower of London and Bishopsgate Roman Baths), we’ll still visit all of the Square Mile's surviving remains. Almost all of Saxon London has disappeared, but its churches, street pattern and place-names survive alongside much more substantial Roman remains. If Saxon London is mostly erased, Roman London is mostly buried and Norman London is mostly fragmentary, all the remnants make for the quintessential City look of ancient juxtaposed with modern.
Timeline of Roman, Saxon and Norman London:
43 AD: Roman conquest of Britain under Emperor Claudius.
47–50: Londinium founded, becoming a major port and commercial centre.
60–61: Boudica's rebellion: Londinium is burned and largely destroyed.
c. 70: London rebuilt; Roman amphitheatre constructed at Guildhall, initially in timber.
c. 100: Londinium reaches its greatest Roman prosperity.
120: Hadrian visits; amphitheatre rebuilt in stone; baths and temples built.
120–150: Cripplegate Roman fort built; London reaches its Roman peak.
120–130: Fire devastates much of Londinium; the city is rebuilt.
190–225: London Wall constructed, enclosing the main city.
240: Mithraeum built beside the Walbrook.
250–275: Riverside wall completes the enclosure of the city.
286–296: Carausius and Allectus overthrow Roman rule in Britannia.
296: Emperor Constantius Chlorus invades and re-establishes imperial control.
313: Christianity officially tolerated throughout the Roman Empire.
350: Towers added to London Wall as Saxon raids threaten.
400-410: Emperor Honorius gradually abandons Britannia. Londinium declines.
C5–C6: Roman London largely abandoned; the walls become ruinous.
C7: Anglo-Saxon trading centre Lundenwic develops where the Strand is.
886: King Alfred refortifies London within the Roman walls (Lundenburh).
994: Vikings under Sweyn Forkbeard begin raids.
1012: St Alphege murdered by Vikings; commemorated by St Alphege church.
1013: Sweyn captures London; King Æthelred forced to flee abroad.
1014: Æthelred (assisted by King Olaf) regains control.
1016: King Cnut the Great of Denmark conquers England.
1042: King Edward the Confessor re-establishes Saxon monarchy.
1042-1065: Edward the Confessor builds Westminster Abbey.
1066: William the Conqueror invades and is crowned at Westminster Abbey.
1066: William allows London to govern itself.
1070–1100: White Tower built, and completed in stone under William II.
1080: Undercroft and original church of St Mary-le-Bow.
C11–C12: Norman London expands within the Roman walls; defences repaired.
1123: Rahere founds St Bartholomew's Hospital and Priory.
c.1150: Norman London established as England's capital and mercantile centre.
The
route
and sights:
Starting at Bank Underground Station, we'll go up Princes Street, then west along Lothbury and Gresham Street and turn right into...
1.
Guildhall Yard and Guildhall Art Gallery: amphitheatre
.
The Yard uses a dark grey ring to preserve the outline of London's Roman amphitheatre, built 74 AD in wood, 31 years after the Roman conquest. Subsequently enlarged, including in 120 AD when it was rebuilt in stone. The enlarged version could hold 6,000 spectators, over a quarter of the population. Spectators would watch displays of gladiatorial combat, animals fighting and criminals being executed. A vertically sliding wooden door, possibly to allow animals to enter, has been carbon-dated. The present Guildhall is medieval, with the Great Hall dating from 1411, but the site has much older associations. The word
guildhall
derives from the Anglo-Saxon
gild
. (Note to self: booking is for 12.00.)
We'll then leave Guildhall Yard by its western side, and follow Love Lane and Oat Lane to Noble Street to see...
2. Noble Street Gardens:
Contains a substantial surviving section of London's Roman and medieval City Wall, incorporated into a small modern garden. The ancient Roman foundations were revealed when bomb damage from the Blitz was being cleared, revealing a fort in the northwest corner of the Roman walls (Cripplegate Fort) that had a garrison of 1000 soldiers and predates the wall.
We'll then continue from Noble Street on to London Wall, then go round the Rotunda and south down St Martins-Le-Grand to then cross Postman's Park heading west to Little Britain which we'll go up towards Cloth Fair where we'll find...
3. Church of St Bartholomew the Great:
Founded in 1123 by Rahere, courtier to Henry I as an Augustinian priory. Rahere was so distressed by the White Ship Disaster (which killed 300 people including Henry I's heir William Adelin, leading to The Anarchy) that he went on pilgrimage to Rome. Attributing his recovery from malaria to St Bartholomew, he founded a priory and a hospital in gratitude. St Bartholomew the Great is one of London's finest medieval survivors. Austere and dark but satisfying, its astonishing Norman fabric provides our walk's clearest architectural encounter with C12 London, and is the best example of Norman architecture outside of the Tower of London. Only the chancel remains, the nave destroyed by Henry VIII's wreckers.
We'll then follow Middle Street and Cloth Street to Aldgate. At The Rotunda we'll enter the Museum of London Car Park where we'll be astonished to find...
4. Fragment of the City Wall, Bay 52:
Just a small piece, but shows history erupting into the drab surroundings.
We'll emerge and proceed along London Wall, where we'll soon find...
5. City Wall Bastion 14:
Mostly medieval, not Roman, but it preserves the footprint and foundations of the earlier Roman defences. Illustrates exceptionally well the continuity and adaptation of London's defensive circuit.
Going into the Barbican Complex (itself named after the Roman Fort), we'll see...
6. Cripplegate Roman Fort Wall:
Dating from 120 AD. The tower is medieval.
Going along Monkwell Square and east along St Alphage Gardens, we'll find...
7. Roman Wall, Salters Garden:
Wall constructed AD 190–225. The Roman masonry here is now largely buried, having been truncated by later medieval rebuilding. Cripplegate Fort is buried beneath the northern wall here. The medieval wall is most of what shows here consisting of ragstone, flint and tile, with a battered outer face. The crenellations and brick diaper pattern is from 1477, added during the Wars of the Roses - the only surviving crenellations on the wall. St Alphage was the Archbishop of Canterbury, murdered by the Vikings in 1012 at Greenwich.
Emerging back on to London Wall (itself loosely following the Roman wall), we'll go east to Wormwood Street and then turn south down St Mary Axe to see...
6. Roman Girl's Grave, 30 St Mary Axe:
At the foot of the Gherkin is a memorial marking the grave of an unidentified Roman girl, 13-17 years old. Her remains were discovered during construction and date from approximately AD 350–400. It is one of the walk's most poignant sites: unlike the amphitheatre, baths and temples, a direct reminder of an individual who lived and died in Roman London.
Heading southeast down Brown's Buildings and Mitre Street, we'll go up St James's Passage to...
7. Aldgate Square:
By the medieval period, the city had outgrown the Roman wall that mostly defines the City of London. By the C18, the Roman gatehouses were is disrepair and impeded traffic, so like Ludgate, Cripplegate and others, Aldgate was pulled down, Aldgate in 1761. The church (1744, by George Dance the Elder) is St Botolph Without Aldgate, 'without' meaning outside of the city wall. St Botolph was a East Anglian saint associated with travellers, hence its location at an exit to the city when it was built originally in 1115. We'll have lunch in the gardens here.
We'll head south down Jewry Street, east down India Street and then turn right down Vine Street to...
8.
Vine Street Roman Wall
:
A substantial section of the city wall, together with the foundations of the only extant Roman bastion (375 AD) and later houses. This portion is in the basement of a modern building, carefully preserved and in 2023 made available for the public to view along with many historic objects. The surviving masonry also illustrates how Roman London continued to shape the medieval and modern city. We are booked in to view the wall and exhibition. (Note to self: booking is for 14.00.)
Continuing down Vine Street, we'll turn right down The Crescent to...
9. Roman Wall, Coopers Row:
A hidden but huge portion, 10.6 m high, although only the lower 6 m is Roman.
Emerging on to Trinity Square, we'll soon see more huge fragments of the Roman wall at...
10. Roman Wall, Wakefield Gardens:
One of the most substantial portions remaining. Most of the building above the red tiles is medieval. The statue is of the Emperor Trajan (ruled 98-117 AD) - a strange choice as he never visited the city unlike his adopted son and first cousin Hadrian.
Then, going under Tower Hill, we'll emerge at...
11. The Tower of London:
William the Conqueror began the White Tower around 1078, transforming this part of the eastern City into a major Norman royal fortress consolidating his power at the corner of the Roman fortifications and the growing mercantile centre. His son, William Rufus (William II) completed the rebuilding of the White Tower in stone. The most important Norman remains on the walk (the chapel of St John the Evangelist is sublime) charges £37 and we won't have time.
We'll walk around the Tower's western side towards Tower Hill, then continue north-west along Gloucester Court to...
12. All Hallows By The Tower:
The church is from the 1950s (by Lord Mottistone) to replace an earlier one destroyed in the Blitz, but the C14 undercroft contains a remarkable survival: a Roman mosaic pavement of a private house, and one what's more which is overlain with a replacement when the original became too wet. The pavement is 7 m below street level, illustrating the accumulation of detritus over time. The undercroft also contains a model of Roman London of 400 AD made in the 1920s. An exhibition of the history of Christianity in the city includes some C11 Saxon stone crosses - the only Saxon remains on the whole walk.
Going southwest down Byward Street and Lower Thames Street, we'll reach...
13. Billingsgate Roman House & Baths:
At 101 Lower Thames Street are the remains of a Roman house and bath complex, first constructed around AD 150. The baths were subsequently enlarged and used for several centuries. The surviving hypocaust illustrates the sophisticated underfloor heating technology of Roman London. Unfortunately, this charges £15 to enter and visiting is by guided tour only.
We'll then walk northwest up Monument Street, north up King William Street, west along Cannon Street, them up Walbrook to...
14. Forgotten Streams:
By sculptor Christina Iglesias, ‘Forgotten Streams’ is located at Bloomberg’s new European Headquarters. It evokes the lost rivers of London, namely the Walbrook along which the Romans built the Mithraeum, and the erasure of features and recycling of space in London.
Further up Walbrook is...
15.
London Mithraeum
:
Beneath Bloomberg's European headquarters is the London Mithraeum, a reconstructed Roman temple dedicated to the cult deity Mithras. The original temple was built in the C3 AD, beside the lost Walbrook River. The atmospheric reconstruction and associated archaeological displays make this one of London's best introductions to Roman religious life. (Note to self: booking is for 15.45.)
Going northwest up Bloomberg Arcade, then crossing Queen Victoria Street and proceeding up Watling Street, we'll turn right up Bow Lane and go through Bow Churchyard to go to...
16. St Mary-le-Bow:
Known for its bells, which feature in the nursery rhyme 'Oranges and Lemons', called back Dick Whittington in 1392 to become Lord Mayor, and define anyone born within earshot of them as true Londoner or Cockney. Wren's magnificent church of 1673 (tower finished 1680) is the third on the site. The earliest remains are a Norman undercroft of 1080. now a cafe.
Walking along Cheapside, we'll either go west to St Paul's or east to Bank Underground Stations to conclude our walk.
My many thanks go to ODL leader Alex Young for introducing me to the Guildhall amphitheatre, Vine Street Roman Wall and the Mithraeum on his excellent walks in the city, and letting me use his photos of the same.

Title: Nottingham Bouldering (Lenton) - MONDAY - Beginners Welcome
Summary:
Swap trainers for climbing shoes and join OutdoorLads for an evening of INDOOR BOULDERING at Nottingham’s newest bouldering venue
NOTE: If you are climbing with us for the first time
, either as an experienced climber or beginner, please send a note to the
Event Leader
telling them about your experience and goals. There is a limit to the number of beginners that we can accommodate at each session. Each beginner needs to be supervised so we need to ensure there are enough experienced climbers to help you out. Climbing is great fun! It's a fab workout, in a social environment, and anyone can do it! Give it a go!
What is Bouldering?
It's a form of climbing where instead of long high routes, the 'problems' tend to be shorter and focus on technique, balance, body positioning and sometimes power. Because of this different emphasis, bouldering doesn't have the hassle of climbing with ropes, harnesses and belaying, which makes it an excellent activity for newcomers to the sport. No wonder it's often regarded as the 'purest' form of climbing.
If you're a seasoned climber you won't need convincing about the benefits of bouldering, but for those who've never climbed more than a staircase, the benefits are wide ranging: from the physical - improved strength, tone, balance, power and coordination; mental - problem solving, focus, concentration and body awareness; to the emotional - relaxation, a sense of achievement and a feeling that mind and body are working together perfectly ('feeling psyched'). On top of all this, bouldering tends to be a very social sport where you can hang out with mates and each have a go as you feel regardless of what level you climb at.
I'm new to Bouldering - can I come along?
If you have never tried bouldering before it is recommended that you have a guided session from the event leader, who will go through everything you will need to know to boulder safely before joining in with the rest of the group.
I've been Bouldering before?
As above, everyone attending the event  must abide by the centre's T&Cs etc. As an experienced boulderer you are responsible for your own safety, actions and involvement at all times. As such, you should use your own judgement in taking up advice given either by OutdoorLads Volunteers or other experienced climbers.
To climb at Nottingham Climbing Centre you will need to:
-     Complete a climbing waiver for the centre (please arrive early to do this the first time, or better still complete it online before you arrive.) You can find the
link
to the waiver and bouldering safety video
here
on Nottingham Climbing Centre's website.
-     Pay the Lifetime Registration Fee - £6.00
-     Pay an Entry Fee directly to the climbing centre - £9.50 (ensure you mention ODL)
-     Hire shoes (if you don’t have your own) - £3.50*
*Equipment hire charges will be waived for your first visit to the centre!
If you have any questions or need any more information just get in touch with the event leader by clicking on their profile below, or take a look at the
My first climbing event page
for more information.
IMPORTANT!
Please note that every person participating should be aware of (and accept) that those members perceived as ‘in charge’ or leading the event are not necessarily qualified, do not need to be qualified, and are not regarded by OutdoorLads, or themselves as ‘technical experts’ but are amateur climbers with some experience and who are happy to impart their knowledge. Any advice given should be considered with this in mind by the recipient.
All those attending the event must also be aware of the centre's own terms and conditions of participation and abide by them, along with any instructions given by the centre’s staff. Everyone must also take responsibility for their own safety while participating in Indoor climbing events.
Photos:
All images supplied by event leaders and used by OutdoorLads with permission.
Difficulty & Distance: Suitable for all abilities. If you're new to bouldering, just let the event leader know and we'll get you started!

Title: NOTTINGHAM Indoor Climbing (Basford) – Beginners welcome
Summary:
Join OutdoorLads at Nottingham Climbing Centre
Climbing evenings are held regularly and we tend to go to the local pub – The Lion for refreshments and a social gathering afterwards where they have a wide variety of beverages both alcoholic and non-alcoholic.
NOTE: If you are climbing with us for the first time
, either as an experienced climber or beginner, please send a note to the
Event Leader
telling them about your experience and goals. There is a limit to the number of beginners that we can accommodate at each session. Each beginner needs to be supervised so we need to ensure there are enough experienced climbers to help you out. Climbing is great fun! It's a fab workout, in a social environment, and anyone can do it! Give it a go!
Nottingham Climbing Centre
Nottingham Climbing Centre is equipped with walls and routes to suit all skill levels and groups of climbers, whether you are a novice looking to try climbing for the first time, or an experienced lead climber, you’ll find an area to challenge you. With 28 Top Ropes routes available as well as 24 Lines of Lead climbing for the more advanced individuals. In addition, 6 auto-belays are available, so there is always the opportunity to climb, even if the numbers don’t match up. The available bouldering walls also provide that extra physical and mental challenge for those looking for something slightly different from rope work. Both Bouldering and Rope Climbing routes range from 4a – 8a.
I'm new to Climbing - can I come along?
If you've never climbed before or need a refresher, the leader will sign you into the climbing centre as a
supervised climber
so that you can come and give it a try (it can be helpful to message the leader to let them know). If you enjoy your climbing experience, and would like to come climbing more regularly, we will also happily show you the ropes and teach you everything you need to know to climb safely.
Do I need to be Supervised as a Climber?
If you answer
NO
to any of the following three questions, then you will need to arrange to be supervised. If you can answer YES to all these questions, you can sign up to this event as normal:
Can you fit a climbing harness correctly?
Can you tie yourself to the end of a rope using the correct knots?
Can you belay another climber correctly and confidently?
To come along, you will need to register via this event page and to climb you will need to pay an entry fee directly to the climbing centre when you arrive, please see their
website
for up-to-date prices. We ask that all members sign up through the event page to make sure the event leader has all information of the members attending.
To climb at Nottingham Climbing Centre you will need to:
-     Complete a climbing waiver for the centre (please arrive early to do this the first time, or better still complete it online before you arrive)
-     Pay the Lifetime Registration Fee - £6.00
-     Pay an Entry Fee directly to the climbing centre - £9.50 (ensure you mention ODL)
-     Hire shoes (if you don’t have your own) - £3.50*
-     Hire a harness (again, if you don’t have your own) - £3.50*
-     Hire shoes and harness - £6.00*
*Equipment hire charges will be waived for your first visit to the centre!
Can I just come along and boulder?
Absolutely! Most of us do roped climbing, but if you prefer bouldering, you can sign yourself in and do it, as long as you can fill in the climbing centre's form correctly, watch their
safety video
and can answer the simple safety questions at reception on your first visit. Meet the group at the start; some others might be bouldering. We will make sure we come and find you when we have our tea break!
If you have any questions or need any more information just get in touch with the event leader by clicking on their profile below, or take a look at the
My first climbing event page
for more information.
IMPORTANT! - Participation Statement
You MUST complete a
Participation Statement
, in addition to booking your event space before attending an OutdoorLads event. You only need to complete this Participation Statement once, not for each event you attend.
Anyone with COVID-19 symptoms, even if they are extremely mild, or who has recently tested positive for Covid-19, is asked not to attend.
Photos:
All images supplied by event leaders and used by OutdoorLads with permission.
Difficulty & Distance: Beginners welcome.

Summary:

Each beginner needs to be supervised so we need to ensure there are enough experienced climbers to help you out. Climbing is great fun! It's a fab workout, in a social environment, and anyone can do it! Give it a go!
What is Bouldering?
It's a form of climbing where instead of long high routes, the 'problems' tend to be shorter and focus on technique, balance, body positioning and sometimes power. Because of this different emphasis, bouldering doesn't have the hassle of climbing with ropes, harnesses and belaying, which makes it an excellent activity for newcomers to the sport. No wonder it's often regarded as the 'purest' form of climbing.
If you're a seasoned climber you won't need convincing about the benefits of bouldering, but for those who've never climbed more than a staircase, the benefits are wide ranging: from the physical - improved strength, tone, balance, power and coordination; mental - problem solving, focus, concentration and body awareness; to the emotional - relaxation, a sense of achievement and a feeling that mind and body are working together perfectly ('feeling psyched'). On top of all this, bouldering tends to be a very social sport where you can hang out with mates and each have a go as you feel regardless of what level you climb at.
I'm new to Bouldering - can I come along?
If you have never tried bouldering before it is recommended that you have a guided session from the event leader, who will go through everything you will need to know to boulder safely before joining in with the rest of the group.
I've been Bouldering before?

Title: Rhaeadr Nantcol - Wild Hills and Waterfalls Camp  2026
Summary:
Join us for a weekend camping at Nantcol Waterfalls, nestled at the foot of the Rhinog mountains.
Far less well known than the areas in the north of the
Eryri National Park
, the Rhinogydd are a wild range of hills in central Snowdonia that are rougher than anything else south of Scotland.The Rhinog mountains are popular with hillwalkers looking for a more isolated, wilder walking experience and we plan to put on a strenuous walk to explore these hills properly.
If mountains aren't for you, Cwm Nantcol has beautiful woods and spectacular waterfalls to explore, and we're also not far from the beach. It may be early October, but it's very often still a lovely time to be camping, and in this year could be especially lovely still!
Showers -
the showers operate on a shower card system which allows a 5-minute shower per card. These cards will be issued to campers at Reception.
Campfires
- Nantcol Waterfalls allow campfires but the site is within a Tree Preservation Area and as such we can only allow the burning of manufactured logs – the collection of deadwood and live wood is not permitted. Fires require the use of Fire Baskets only, which can be bought on site or hired from Reception. We will sort a communal fire.
Mobile signal
- signal is weak at this site but, if you're desperate to get online, you can pay for wifi access. Alternatively, if you venture 100 metres up the hill on the same side as the waterfalls you should obtain 4 bars from most signal providers.
Dogs
- the site permits dogs with well behaved owners. There is a charge of £4 per dog for the weekend payable on arrival to the site in cash. Dogs must be on a lead at all times when on site as this is a sheep farm - no exceptions can be made.
Music
- This campsite does not allow music to be played.
Campervans, Caravans, Motorhomes
: campervans and motorhomes are welcome at no extra charge, but no electric hook-up pitches are available. (Apologies for the earlier confusion before this amendment was made :) )

Title: Bouldering NORTH WALES - Beginners welcome
Summary:
Join OutdoorLads For An Evening of INDOOR BOULDERING in NORTH WALES!
This event is intended as a safe space for the LGBTQ+ community; everyone will be warmly welcomed
Bouldering is a form of climbing that focuses on shorter "problems" emphasising technique, balance, body positioning, and sometimes power, rather than long, high routes. Without the need for ropes, harnesses, and belaying, bouldering is an accessible activity for newcomers and is often considered the "purest" form of climbing.
Bouldering offers a wide range of benefits, including:
Physical:
Improved strength, tone, balance, power, and coordination.
Mental:
Enhanced problem-solving, focus, concentration, and body awareness.
Emotional:
Relaxation, a sense of achievement, and a feeling of mind-body connection.
Bouldering is also a fantastic way to meet new people and build lasting friendships, as it's an inherently social sport where climbers share tips and strategies to conquer the routes.
New to Bouldering?
If you're new to bouldering, it is recommended that you have a guided session from the event leader to learn the basics of safe bouldering. The leader can then introduce you to the rest of the group where you can refine your newly learnt skills in a social environment.
Experienced Boulderer?
If you’re new to climbing with ODL, the leader will help to introduce you to the rest of the group so you can explore the centre together.
You are responsible for your own safety and actions while bouldering. Please use your own judgement when accepting advice from OutdoorLads Volunteers or other experienced climbers, regardless of your bouldering experience.
Ready to boulder?
You will need to sign up on the ODL event page. We would ask you to do this each time so that the leader has access to important information
If you are not already registered with The Boardroom Climbing centre you will need to do so when you arrive. Maybe arrive a little earlier to do so.
When you arrive at the centre you will need to pay for entry and hire climbing shoes if you don't own a pair.
Get bouldering! You’ll find most of the group already bouldering so feel free to join them. If you’re new to bouldering with ODL, the leader will be looking out for you so if you spot them, please go speak with them first.
Any questions?
If you have any questions, please contact the leader directly.

Summary:

Title: Where the Crane meets planes. Walk, nature & picnic at LHR
Summary:
I've been visiting the viewing area by Myrtle Avenue, by the landing lights for years, to watch the planes landing at Heathrow and often thought it would be great to get an ODL group together for a picnic and to enjoy the big jets. I know there are a lot of guys like me who like aviation, or maybe you fancy doing something a bit different. Add to that a flat, easy walk along the River Crane from Twickenham, and I think its a fun little day out.
You can come for the walk or picnic or both!
The Walk
Join me on this easy flat linear walk from Twickenham station following the River Crane as it meanders to Heathrow Airport. There's an optional walk around a small nature reserve by Crane Park.
The walk route map can be viewed in OS Maps
here
.
Points of interest
River Crane
The River Crane, a tributary of the River Thames, runs 8.5 miles (13.6 km). It forms the lower course of Yeading Brook. It adjoins or passes through three London boroughs: Hillingdon, Hounslow and Richmond upon Thames.
Crane Park & Shot Tower
Crane Park is a 30 hectare public park next to the River Crane. The Hounslow Gunpowder Works opened in the late 1760s in what is now the western end of the park. Crane Park Island was created to provide a mill pond for the water to drive the machinery. There were many explosions and the Shot Tower is now thought to have been a windmill for recirculating water to power the mills, rather than a shot tower for making lead shot.
The licence to manufacture gunpowder was withdrawn in 1927, and part of the site was sold to Twickenham Council, which turned it into Crane Park. This opened in 1935. The Shot Tower (now officially the Brick Tower) is a Grade II listed building.
Crane Park Island Nature Reserve
There is a short circular walk of the reserve for those who wish to visit.
Heathrow Airport
The airport was opened on 25 March 1946 as London Airport; taking on the role of the UKs main International Airport from Croydon. It was renamed Heathrow Airport in September 1966. The airport's Central Terminal Area (CTA) was designed by Sir Frederick Gibberd, who set out the terminals and central-area buildings, including the control tower and the multi-faith Chapel of St George's.
The airport consists of Terminals 2, 3, 4 & 5 and handles 1,300 flight movements daily and connects passengers to around 230 direct destinations across 85 countries, served by over 80 airlines.
The Picnic
The plan is to have a picnic at the end of the walk at the viewing area known as Myrtle Avenue. What 3 words:
///yarn.rested.stack
We should be able to see aircraft landing on runway 27L before they switch to 27R at 15.00. However the runway alteration programme can change depending on the wind direction, but hopefully we'll get some take off's or landings.
You can of course just come for the picnic. We will aim to be at the viewing area by 13.30 or thereabouts.
If you only wish to attend the picnic, please sign up as usual but add in the comments below that you are  only attending the picnic.
You might want to bring a blanket, rug or something to sit on as the ground is dry and dusty. Bring food and drink with you or the BP petrol station 2 mins walk is well stocked. There is also a toilet here.

Title: Llanberis: heritage and natural beauty
Summary:
The landscape of Llanberis in the heart of Eryri is like nowhere else. The town sits at the junction of two lakes Llyn Padarn and Llyn Peris and lies at the foot of Yr Wyddfa the highest mountain in England and Wales.
In the past is was a place where hundreds of men exported thousands of tons of slate through the ports of Caernarfon and Bangor. Nowadays it is a centre for outdoor activities of all sorts, and the starting point of two steam powered railways, the most famous being the one that ascends Yr Wyddfa.
The area may carry the scars of two centuries of slate quarrying but it still provides attractive foregrounds for some of the finest and most famous views. Quite often, the best views of mountains are not from the summits, nor the valleys, but from halfway above on the opposite side as is the case with this walk.
This event is more of a multi facetted day out as well as a good walk. Our journey combines the stark and remarkable slate workings of the Dinorwig quarries, views of the lakes and mountains, a castle visit and a small museum.
We will start with a look at the remains of Castle Dolbadarn (free entry) - one of the original Welsh castles built by Llewyn ap Iowerth to defend the are from the marauding Anglo Saxons.
Then there's a pretty steep 1 mile uphill incline passing the famous Anglesey Barracks, a ruined row of miners cottages seen on many postcards and biscuit tins.
The climb rewards us with a truly superb viewpoint. After this we will go on to see some of the shear rock faces and extraordinary mine workings which are on a vast scale and popular with daring climbers.
The route then drops back down through the forest above Llyn Peris and gives us the opportunity for a quick visit into a museum which was a hospital to treat wounded quarry workers and contains exhibits of historical medical equipment and practices – a fascinating glimpse into the past. (free entry)
Dogs
are welcome to join us on this event but please note the following:
This route may pass through areas with livestock.  Your dog needs to be well behaved and be on a lead at times. It must not affect other member's enjoyment of the event.  There may be stiles to carry your dog across. Your dog needs to have the stamina to keep up with the group.

Title: SE500: The White Horse of Uffington
Summary:
This walk has been conceived, written & illustrated by
Frankie Bruce
, who has pioneered the idea of challenging hill walks in the relatively flat south-east of England for OutdoorLads. Our grateful thanks to Frankie for preparing the event for us.
-----------------------------------------------------------------
This is a spectacular walk taking in the very best of the White Horse hills, on mostly good tracks. The walk takes in ancient history as well as manor houses and passes race horse gallops. Do have a look at Frankie's photos and the special video he has prepared for this walk below.
This walk is part of the SE500 series, covering a slightly longer distance and more ascent than your average hill walk. In total, over 500 metres of ascent are covered, which should help you burn off an average of 2100 calories.
The walk begins with a circle of Woolstone Wells valley, and a steep ascent onto the
Dragon’s Hill
. This is a mound which is bare on top, exposing the chalk, as no grass will grow here. Legend has it this is because the blood of a dragon was spilled here.
We then circle the
White Horse of Uffington
to gain the very best views of this site. This is a huge chalk figure of a horse in the hillside, dating from the Bronze Age around 4000 years ago. It is 114 metres long – a colossal and well-known site. It is thought it was of importance to the ancient Celts. Another rumour was that the horse was created by King Alfred in celebration of a battle victory, but it has actually been dated as much older than that.
There is evidence of other fortifications in the smaller humps nearby, which date from the Iron Age. Our route climbs onto
Uffington Castle
with its fortification mounds, itself an Iron Age hill fort which was built on top of the Bronze Age one.
Descending from the fort, the route crosses ancient ditches below Woolstone Down Gallops, a training ground for the finest race horses. The route continues over gently rolling hills and fields to Weathercock Hill to Ashdown Park (National Trust). The house was built by Lord William of Craven in the 1660s. We follow paths through the woods with a good view of the house.
We then turn north and head up over Odstone Down and continue for two miles over rolling downs. Where the track turns left, look across the field to
Wayland's Smithy
, an atmospheric neolithic warrior’s long barrow burial ground. This is about 5500 years old! Wayland or Wolund was named after a god in Norse mythology.
The route descends to
Ashbury village
, with its quaint thatched cottages, pub, village shop and café and manor house. There may be an opportunity for an afternoon break stop here. We then ascend most of the way up Odstone Hill with good views north west.
The ornate Compton Beauchamp House, a Baroque style stately home, was originally a moated manor house built by Sir Thomas Fettiplace in 1507. Nearly there! The return rises above Woolstone Village up the hill to start, using the path in the access land to the left of the road.

Title: 'A Haunt of Ancient Peace' - Parham in Autumn
Summary:
"Nothing at Parham is superfluous, nothing unloved. It is a house of magic." (Simon Jenkins,
England's Thousand Best Houses
)
"An English house - gray twilight pour'd / On dewy pastures, dewy trees, / Softer than sleep - all things in order stored, / A haunt of ancient peace." (Tennyson,
The Palace of Art
)
Simon Jenkins considers Parham House to be not just among England's thousand best, or even among its hundred best. He considers it to be among its twenty best, on a par with Chatsworth, Blenheim and Hardwick Hall. To me it is superior to those, eschewing military pomp and showy boastfulness; 'a haunt of ancient peace' indeed. Built in 1577 before the era of Elizabethan 'prodigy houses' like Hardwick, it is straightforward and sober in design, but the interiors are Elizabethan and Jacobean at their finest. Sunday 11 October will be the last time it opens in 2026, and we'll
walk
three and a half picturesque downland miles to get there from Amberley Station.
The chief points of interest at
Parham House
and Park are:
The deer park, which is a chase of big trees and bracken with the bare South Downs behind as a dramatic backdrop.
A classic Elizabethan E-shaped plan, although the east wing has been much altered and was restored to its Tudor design in the twentieth century.
The Great Hall with bay windows from floor to ceiling, flooding the heraldry and portraits with light.
A picture collection of Tudor royalty and statesmen, including the famous portrait of the doomed Henry, Prince of Wales being pursued by winged Time from 1611.
The Saloon, designed and decorated in 1790, so bringing the Georgian era to the building.
The Green Room, dedicated to Sir Joseph Banks, explorer and president of The Royal Society. His portrait is by Joshua Reynolds and there are paintings of exotic animals by George Stubbs.
The Long Gallery, which stretches the length of the South Front and was designed for indoor exercise. The vista down the gallery is superb.
The gardens are seven acres of Pleasure Grounds, laid out in the 18th century, with a lake, a brick and turf maze and many specimen trees.
The Walled Garden contains romantic wide herbaceous borders, a rose garden, a cut flower garden, a vegetable garden, and an orchard. The Greenhouse has a fine display of pelargoniums.
The finest collection of historic needlework outside of London.
Fresh floral arrangements in every room for the duration of the season.
If we set off from Amberley at 11.00, we should reach Parham by 12.20. The gardens will be open then, so we can explore those and have lunch. The house opens at 14.00.
The cost of entrance to the house and gardens is £15.88 with Gift Aid or £14.43 without it. Parham is privately owned, so unfortunately National Trust or English Heritage memberships won't be of use. Historic Houses members gain free admission, however, and RHS members can gain free admission to the gardens, and the house for an extra £4.

Title: Baslow to Rowsley - DVH Way Section 3
Summary:
The Derwent Valley Trust
was set up in 1996 to promote the history, arts, wildlife and leisure opportunities that surround the river Derwent along its 55 mile course through Derbyshire.
The Derwent Valley Heritage Way
takes us from Ladybower Reservoir in the Peak District National Park to its end at Derwent Mouth where it flows into the River Trent near Shardlow. The Duke of Devonshire opened the walk at Chatsworth House in 2003.
The route takes us through the Chatsworth estate, Derbyshire dales, towns, villages, canals and many points of interests through the
Derwent Valley Mills World Heritage Site
. There are plenty of pubs and tea shops for refreshments along the way. The route follows the riverside path through Derby City and continues southeastwards to the historic inland port of Shardlow. Journey’s end is at Derwent Mouth where the Derwent flows into the River Trent.
The route is divided into eight sections of between  ~13 km (8 miles) and ~17 km (10.5 miles), each with a clear public transport solution. All, except the first section, are linear routes. We park at the end, travel to the start, and walk back to our cars. Sections 5, 6, 7 are brilliantly served by the East Midlands Railway Derwent Valley Line
(Derby–Matlock, hourly), which runs almost parallel to the trail the whole way. For sections (2, 3, 4 and 8), we use local buses.
Each section is a walk in itself. Join one or more, as you wish, or walk all eight sections to complete the whole route through Derbyshire. Please ask other attendees for a lift if you need one.
Section 3 - Baslow to Rowsley ~14 km (8.7 miles) Total ascent 199 m (653 ft)
The highlight of this section of the Way is the impressive
Chatsworth Estate
, with its house set in an extensive deer park landscaped by Lancelot (Capability) Brown. The 4th Duke of Devonshire (1720-64) had a channel cut across an S-bend upstream of the House to straighten the river and deal with intermittent flooding.
The route takes us through the stable yard, where refreshments are available, then we climb up to the top of the Cascade and across to the hunting lodge from where there are great views across the estate. The Emperor Fountain, which sends up a 88 m (290 feet) jet of water, is one of the park’s striking features.
Edensor village originally straggled across the valley so the 4th Duke removed a mill and some cottages to make room for the new 'one arch' bridge. In the 19th century, the 6th Duke and Joseph Paxton had the rest of Edensor demolished and rebuilt where it is today. Each house is a different design. The single house opposite the Edensor gates was spared because it was occupied by an old man at the time and the Duke did not want to disturb him.
The enlarged 14th century church of St Peter contains, among others features, a memorial to Paxton, the tomb of two sons of Bess of Hardwick, everlasting memorial flowers sent by Queen Victoria, and the grave of Kathleen Kennedy, sister of President John F Kennedy, who died in an air crash in 1948.
As the route winds through the estate south to Rowsley, there are close views of the Derwent.
At the end of this section we visit Caudwell’s Mill, a 19th-century grade II listed roller flour mill with pre-1914 machinery powered by two water turbines. There are several craft outlets and a shop on site selling different types of flour.

Title: SE500 Cromer (with easier option)
Summary:
This walk consists of 2 parts:
Part 1 - Moderate walk Cromer to Sheringham
- 9.1K (6 miles) then get the train back.
Part 2 -(optional) SE500 - walk back to Cromer via a different route
- total 20.6K (13 miles) and 500m ascent.
Everyone
will walk
Part 1
first, then you can choose whether to continue with
Part 2
or get the train back to Cromer.
You are most welcome to join this beautiful walk taking in sweeping panoramas of the Norfolk coast, the highest point in the county, as well as the Cromer Ridge and woodlands. New members are welcome and will find this a friendly, small group walk which provides a great introduction to Outdoorlads.
Cromer
is known as the gem of the Norfolk Coast. It’s Victorian Pier and Pavilion Theatre are prominent landmarks. Brightly painted beach huts line the promenade, whilst poppies adorn the hilltops beside the coast. After taking in the view from the coastal hill, we follow paths inland to Incleborough Hill.
Incleborough Hill
is a common west of Cromer, rising 79 metres above sea level, has excellent views across the landscape and out to sea. Glaciers from Norway melted at the end of an Ice Age, depositing gravel here which made the hill. Today, buzzards, honey buzzards, sparrowhawks, and kestrels can be spotted.
Next, we top
Beacon Hill
, the county top (highest point) in Norfolk at 105m. It is known as a Roman Camp by locals. Scenic panoramas of the coastline can be seen from here. Nightjar birds can sometimes be spotted. This area forms the Cromer Ridge.
The
Cromer Ridge
was used to defend the coast from invasion over the centuries. Beacon fires were lit on the ridge to signal to other villages along the coast that invaders were coming. These were used since Roman times then later to warn of the Spanish Armada under Elizabeth I. In places on the ridge there is evidence of World War Two: earthworks, practice trenches, weapons pits, and gun placements.
Iron smelting pits dating from Saxon times were found by archaeologists here. Apparently, the site was very good for blowing, using the coastal air. Returning to the coast,
Beeston Bump
provides a good view heading towards Sheringham. There was a listening station here to detect U-Boat signals during World War Two.
We follow the coastal path to the High Street where we will stop for lunch.
You can choose
here whether to continue with
Part 2
or get the train back to Cromer.
Sheringham to Cromer trains run hourly at roughly XX45 minutes past the hour and take 8 minutes, single fare £4.10.
After lunch,
Part 2
follows a different route back to Cromer, which is inland and goes over more of the Cromer Ridge, with some steeper parts balanced with good tracks. Taking parts 1 and 2 together, this walk adds up to an SE500: 500m of ascent over about 13 miles, burning off an average of 2100 calories.

Title: Autumnal Weekend On The Slopes Of Skiddaw
Summary:
At 470m above sea level, Skiddaw House is the highest hostel in Britain. It was built around 1829 as a 'Keeper's lodge' and grouse shooting base for George Wyndham, the third Earl of Egremont. The building was originally divided into two separate dwellings; one side for the gamekeeper and his family and the other for a shepherd's family. The Earl and his shooting parties also had a few rooms to stay in when they came to visit. In 1986 the two dwellings were converted into the hostel it is today.
Skiddaw House operated as a youth hostel from 1987 until 2002, when it closed and began to fall into disrepair again. But with the help of the previous hostel manager, many volunteers and the Skiddaw House Foundation, the hostel was renovated and reopened in 2007. The building retains many original features, which combined with its interesting history and remote location make the hostel a unique place to stay.
One of the great features of Skiddaw House is its remote location, offering stunning views of the surrounding Lakeland fells. This venue is an OutdoorLads favourite and is truly special, right from the moment you park up you'll understand why this is so glorious!
However, the remote nature of the hostel means it is lacking the mod cons we may be used to, such as heating. Don't panic, there are a number of open fires throughout the building which helps keep it warm, but the bedrooms do not have any heating. Full bedding of 15tog duvets and pillow are provided but some may prefer to pack their own sleeping bag. Boots are also not allowed to be worn inside so we recommend packing slippers too!
Itinerary
Friday Afternoon/Evening -
Arrive at the car park for 15:00, meet the rest of the group and we will hike up to the hostel together,
sharing the load of weekend food supply bags
. Please have your head torch handy in case we start to lose the light! Once we have arrived and found our beds and settled in a bit, we'll have a briefing and dish out the traditional OutdoorLads buffet.
Important: If you're not able to arrive at the car park for 15:00, please message the event Leader at least a week before the event and we'll see what we can do. The walk in from the car park is over an hour long. Depending who signs up, we may be able to organise a second walk-in to the hostel with prior notice. There's no phone signal at the parking location or the venue. I'll share a route map from car park to hostel prior to the event in case of emergency.
Saturday Day -
A simple cold breakfast will be available. The main activity of the day will be a bit of a Wainwright epic, as we tick off up to 5 "Wainwrights," with the main attraction being Skiddaw (931m) on our hike. I expect we'll cover 14km in no more than 7 hours, with a total ascent of 1000m. However, if we're moving a bit slower or there is appetite to cut the walk short, we will be able to cut out some sections.
Saturday Evening -
Pop your feet up and unwind from the day's walk. We'll have a hearty evening meal to warm us back up, followed by some games and good laughs. While the hostel has a few, if you have a favourite travel size board/card game why not bring it?
Sunday -
Breakfast is provided once more then we'll all band together to tidy and clean up the hostel to how we found it (takes no time at all with so many) before we need to vacate by 11am. Once done we will take everything we brought back to the car park and then people might want to head home, or into Keswick for an afternoon touristing. I'll aim to lead a quick nip up to Blencathra (868m) via Hall's Fell Ridge, and back down to the car park. This is around 8km, 700m ascent, and should take around 4 hours.
Other information
Dogs:
The event leader very much welcomes well behaved, quiet dogs on this event. They should be able to cope with and enjoy a long mountain walk, be friendly with other dogs and people in a fairly small hostel, not go upstairs whilst wet, and be exceptionally well behaved around food. The venue has capped the number of dogs at three, and they and their humans will be assigned to one room, leaving other bedrooms available for humans only. Contact
support@outdoorlads.com
to reserve a dog space.
Food:
Please note that all food/drink provided will be plant-based. Whilst I encourage you all to embrace plant-based foods for the weekend, you are welcome to bring whatever buffet contributions you like. You'll also need to bring a packed lunch.
Skiddaw House requires a 1 hour hike to access it from the car park. To ensure everyone arrives safely we ask that all attendees meet at the car park for 3pm Friday so that we can hike up together. You will need to carry everything you need for the weekend including food and drink, plus a modest bag of supplies from the event leader in one trip - so pack light!
