Title: Cheddar Gorge, Velvet Bottom, Beacon Batch and Rowberrow
Summary:
This is a 17km circular route, starting in Cheddar, and walking up the western edge of Cheddar gorge, located within the Mendip Hills National Landscape.  The walk commences with the toughest ascent of the day, and passes the lookout tower and pulpit rock, where you can get far reaching views right across the Somerset levels towards the Quantock hills in the distance, as well as cliff top views down into the gorge itself. From here we descend down to the flower rich limestone grassland of the Black Rock and Velvet Bottom Nature reserves.  We then ascend up to the Beacon Batch trig point, which at 325 metres, is the highest point within the Mendip Hills, where weather permitting,  we should get spectacular views across North Somerset and the Bristol channel, before dropping down to the woodland of Rowberrow Warren, and from there returning to the start point in Cheddar.
This walk is approximately 17km in length, has some very steep sections, with a total height gain of 460 metres.

Title: Wargrave, Hurley & the Dew Drop: Boys, Boots, Boats & Beer
Summary:
Please note that the
capacity for this event is currently set at 20,
but I may look to expand to 25-30 as we look to promote this one at Reading Pride for potential new members in the region. If capacity is reached please add yourself to the waitlist and I will revisit after Reading Pride on 5th Sept.
Overview:
Lace up your boots for a 12.3 mile adventure that showcases some of the best of the mid Berkshire countryside. Starting in the upmarket riverside village of Wargrave, we'll meander through peaceful fields of wheat and sheep, shaded woodland and quiet country paths before dropping downhill and joining the Thames Path for a beautiful stretch alongside the river. As we reach the halfway point, we'll arrive in the historic village of Hurley where we will stop for a lunch break.
Refuelled and ready, we'll leave the river and Hurley behind and head back uphill into rolling farmland and extensive woodland. After a couple of miles with the worst of the climbing out of the way, out of the blue we will reach the Dew Drop Inn, a hidden gem tucked away in the woods and the perfect excuse for an afternoon drink (hydration is important, after all!).
From the Dew Drop we have the final four-mile stroll back to Wargrave, including one more long but gradual climb, where tired feet, rosy cheeks and plenty of laughs will mark the end of the day packed with riverside views, woodland trails, good company and and iconic pub stop. 🍺🥾🌳
The Route:
Starting from Wargrave Station, we will initially walk through the old part of the village, past the church and cross the High Street. We will then proceed through Upper Wargrave, with it's more modern housing estates, before getting to the village boundary and open countryside.
Initially we walk through fields and then an extensive section through woodland (Bottom Boles Wood), taking the Chilterns Way/Berkshire extension for some of the way. After climbing up into the small hamlet of Warren Row, we then take a long, straight and gradually downhill route down the valley towards the Thames, and after crossing a main road we take a lane to eventually join the Thames Path.
We then walk east along the Thames Path for about 1.25 miles until we get to Hurley, where we will stop for lunch. There are benches by the river and also in the village centre. After lunch we will continue to walk North through the village, crossing the main road again, and then it's initially an uphill section back out of the Thames Valley through fields and woodland.
When we get to the scenic Ashley Hill forest we will have a pub stop at the iconic Dew Drop Inn, and afterwards will continue through the forest. We continue through sections of fields and woodland until we get to another extensive area of woodland and will take the wide Knowl Hill bridleway along a gradual but long uphill section to the top of Bowsey Hill. From the top we continue through more woodland and at the fringes eventually re-join the route that we took out of Wargrave where we will retrace our steps back to and through the village.
The route can be found
here
:
The Sights:
Wargrave:
is a Thames-side village in Berkshire, nestled where the River Thames meets the River Loddon. Dating back to Saxon times, the village features a several historic buildings centred around its attractive High Street and the 13th-century St Mary's Church, with parts of the church reflecting centuries of architectural development. The village is also home to the Grade II-listed Wargrave War Memorial, designed by the distinguished architect Sir Edwin Lutyens and unveiled in 1922.
Hurley:
is one of Berkshire's most historic Thames-side villages, with origins dating back to Saxon times. The village is best known for the remains of Hurley Priory, founded in 1086 as a Benedictine monastery, parts of which survive within the present-day St Mary the Virgin Church, Hurley. Adjacent to the priory stands The Olde Bell, established in 1135 as the monastery's guesthouse and widely regarded as one of England's oldest continuously operating inns. The village also has strong links to the Glorious Revolution, with nearby Ladye Place serving as a secret meeting place for those who supported the accession of William III.
The Dew Drop Inn:
is nestled in the heart of Ashley Hill Forest and often described as a "little pub in the woods". It's a Grade II-listed country pub that has welcomed travellers and locals since the 18th century. Built in the mid-1700s from traditional flint, chalk and red brick, the inn retains many original features, including exposed beams, open fireplaces and its intimate woodland character. Historically, it served as an important stopping place for forestry workers, horse riders and travellers crossing the surrounding countryside.
Ashley Hill Forest:
is an expanse of ancient woodland, once part of the historic woodlands that covered much of the Chiltern foothills. The forest combines ancient broadleaf woodland with areas of conifer plantation that are now being carefully restored to their natural character, and is popular with walkers, cyclists and horse riders. A notable landmark is its impressive Giant Sequoia, believed to be one of the tallest trees in Berkshire.
Dogs:
Well-behaved dogs are welcome, there will be a few areas where we are walking along or crossing roads but the majority of the walk is in open countryside where dogs can be let off the lead. Please abide by the Countryside Code (
https://tinyurl.com/rlqvp3h
) and remember not everyone loves dogs as much as you do so be mindful of other members.
Photos:
All photos the leader's own (taken in June 2026), with permission given to OutdoorLads for use.
Difficulty & Distance: 12.3 miles, good condition paths of grass, dirt and tarmac, moderately undulating with a total ascent of 275 meters

Title: Jack and Jill went Up the Hill, the Lads Likewise to See Her
Summary:
Jack and Jill, in case you are wondering, are a pair of windmills on the Downs behind Brighton, he a brick tower mill, she a wooden post mill. Jack is currently indisposed: he's lost his sails and dome while restoration work goes on, but Jill has just been fully restored and now opens on Sundays in August and September, hence this walk. Even if you've seen the windmills lots of times before, seeing inside Jill, seeing the Grade I-listed Elizabethan mansion that is Danny House, seeing the views of the Weald to the north and Brighton to the south, seeing the fare in the tearooms of Ditchling and seeing your OutdoorLads mates should be enough reasons to venture up the hill again.
The sights:
Danny House:
A Grade I-listed Elizabethan mansion at the foot of Wolstonbury Hill, built in 1593–95 by George Goring on the site of an earlier medieval house. Designed in the shape of the letter 'E' in honour of Queen Elizabeth I, it is an outstanding example of Elizabethan architecture, with a monumental red-brick east front and an elegant Georgian south façade added in the 1720s. During the First World War, Prime Minister David Lloyd George lived at Danny House, where meetings of the Imperial War Cabinet were held. On 13 October 1918, ministers agreed the armistice terms to be offered to Germany, a decision that helped bring the war to an end. The surrounding parkland retains ancient trees, including the celebrated "Danny Old One" oak (perhaps the oldest oak tree in the Sussex Weald with a girth of 9.9 metres), and historic woodland.
Wolstonbury Hill:
A 58.9-hectare biological Site of Special Scientific Interest. Rising to 206 metres, it extends northwards into the Weald off the South Downs, offering extensive views across both the South Downs and the Weald. Notable landmarks visible from the summit include the Clayton Windmills, Ditchling Beacon, Devil's Dyke and Chanctonbury Ring. The hill is owned and managed by the National Trust, and part of it is designated as a Scheduled Monument.
Jack and Jill Windmills:
Jill is a beautifully restored wooden post mill dating from 1821, hauled from Seven Dials in Brighton in 1852 (by 86 Sussex oxen, some sources say) and open to visitors on the day of our walk. Nearby Jack, a brick tower mill built in 1866, remains structurally intact but is currently without its cap and sails while restoration work continues. Admission to Jill is free, with donations welcomed, and refreshments are usually available. For more information, click
here
.
Ditchling:
Built on a crossroads which has the C13 St Margaret's Church high above it, it is very pretty in flint, timber, brick and tile. Interesting buildings include: 'Anne of Cleves' House', which was given by Henry VIII to his fourth queen as part of her marriage annulment settlement; and 'Sopers', the home of wood engraver, stone sculptor, type designer and sexual abuser Eric Gill, which became an artistic community and inspired a museum of the arts and crafts. This was designed in 2014 by Adam Richards Architects. Noted Ditchling residents include Raymond Briggs, Donald Sinden and Dame Vera Lynn. Ditchling also has a good supply of pubs and tearooms of which we'll make use. Just outside Ditchling at Keymer is another windmill, Oldland Windmill, a wooden post mill from 1703, restored and functioning.
The
route
(please click the link to see it at the Ordnance Survey)
:
We'll follow the B2166, walking on the pavement west out of Hassocks, before turning south down New Way Lane before quickly taking a footpath to Danny House along its avenue. We'll get back on to New Way Lane before turning west along a bridleway and then south up Wolstonbury Hill. Descending the hill we'll turn east towards Rockrose. Emerging on to the the A273 we'll head south using its pavement to pick up the South Downs Way to Clayton Windmills, have lunch, then head further east and then north to descend the Downs along the Sussex Border Path. We'll then reach Ditchling for tea and cake. Leaving the village by heading northwest along Lodge Hill Lane, we'll pass Oldland Windmill and reach Mill Lane. Ockley Lane will take us back into Hassocks and Grand Avenue back to the station.
Dogs:
I love having dogs on my walks and this walk is very suitable for them unless it's really hot. There will be some stiles and livestock, plus some roads to walk along. A dog off the lead must be obedient.

Title: Autumn retreat to The Gower
Summary:
Join Ben for a quiet and relaxed weekend on The Gower Peninsular.
This early autumn weekend is the perfect chance to get some fresh sea air in peaceful countryside.  OutdoorLads hostels are a great way to quickly meet new friends and find out about what we do. Attending your first hostel event could be a daunting experience if you don’t know what’s going to happen so why not have a read of our '
My First Hostel Event
' guide.
Kilvrough Manor is hidden away in its own wooded grounds in the South of the Gower making for a warm and comfortable retreat as Autumn sets in.  With three rooms to socialise in along with a fire pit area there's plenty of space to play board games or chat away and make new friends aswell as catching up with old ones over the weekend.  Please note that the hostel has a no nut policy.
Friday evening:
Arrive, settle in and meet with fellow ODLers.  A simple evening meal (included in the event cost) will be provided followed by a welcome meeting.  The rest of the evening is yours to enjoy.
Saturday:
After breakfast (included in the event cost) we'll head out for a 10 mile walk taking in views of Pobble Bay. You will need a relatively good level of fitness for the walk.
Please bring a packed lunch
and maybe a flask of hot drink if it's cold.
If you don't fancy coming on the walk, you can choose to stay in the hostel or explore nearby Oxwich Bay, Port Eynon or Rhossili.
Saturday evening:
Relax and socialise or help out preparing the 2 course evening meal (included in the event cost) which we'll all enjoy.
Sunday
After breakfast we'll help clean and tidy away leaving the hostel as we found it.  After that you can explore The Gower before heading home.

Title: For Halloween: Gothic Ruins, Graveyards and Ghost Trains
Summary:
Six hours or so hours after the witching hour (which is apparently between 3 and 4 in the morning) we'll start our walk. Our route to reach some Halloween hallmarks (castles, graveyards, relics) will proceed along trackways (or, if very muddy, quiet tarmac lanes) and go to West Grinstead, home to some vintage railway infrastructure, and Knepp Park, home to Tamworth pigs, longhorn cattle and Exmoor ponies. If the countryside all around looks like a tidy, landscaped park, then the park itself looks increasingly unkempt as the livestock graze and biodiversity increases. All in all, urbanity in the smart houses, rusticity in the remote farms, fantasy in the old remains, felicity in the autumn colours.
The sights:
Christ's Hospital:
An independent school founded for poor boys by Edward VI in 1553, but moved from the City of London to Sussex in the C19. Around 900 girls and boys (whose education is still paid for by bursaries) who wear Tudor-style uniforms of dark blue serge with yellow stockings. Main buildings are huge and in a simplified Gothic-Elizabethan style by Aston Webb, begun 1893, finished 1902.
West Grinstead:
The topographer Ian Nairn is worth quoting: 'Halfway between Horsham and the Downs, at a point where the Weald has opened out and become more park-like, with trim hedges rather than copses. The Burrells with their pair of Nash houses [Knepp Castle and West Grinstead Park] and attendant landscaping have given it a character unlike anywhere else in Sussex: The Weald has been at first tamed, then let back, on a leash as it were, to be wild within limits.' Gateland's Farm is C17, Grade II-listed, gabled, tiled and timber-framed but with an alarmingly leaning chimney. St George's Church is by the River Adur and has stone slab roofs and a low, shingled spire. Early Norman north aisle, the rest is C13 but with a C15 timber porch. Good monuments such as brasses and busts by Rysbrack and Flaxman. Glebe Cottage is C18 and Glebe House is c1600. West Grinstead Station was on the Beeching-cut Horsham-Shoreham line and retains platforms, signage, signals and a British Railways Mark 1 carriage in green Southern livery.
Knepp Estate:
Old Knepp Castle is a fragment of an C11 century Norman keep, 10m tall, with a mound and a small motte. New Knepp Castle was built by John Nash in 1809. Stucco, not stone, and in a flamboyant and irregular design. Burnt in 1904 and rebuilt exactly. Park by Humphrey Repton. The website states about the estate:
'
3,500 acres in the heart of the Sussex Weald. Knepp Estate...has been owned by the Burrells for over 220 years...Until recently most of the land was devoted to traditional arable and dairy farming but in 2001 we shifted our focus entirely and embarked on a series of regeneration and restoration projects aimed at nature conservation - or 'rewilding', as it has come to be known. We are still farming, just in a less intensive way - producing organic, pasture-fed meat from free-roaming herds of animals within the Wildland project.' We'll mostly just see the parkland.
Dragon's Green:
A hamlet of pretty weatherboarded and timber-framed cottages but also some 1950s houses which give a suburban feel. The George and Dragon Pub is very pleasant. Handsome Newbuildings Place is 'Artisan Mannerist' in style, dated 1683, stone and brick built with a Dutch gable and home to Wilfred Scawen Blunt, author, poet, traveller and breeder of Arab horses, who is buried in the grounds.
Dogs:
I love having dogs on my walks and this walk is suitable for them. It is of moderate length, but there will be fields with livestock and a number of stiles and roads to negotiate. A dog must be obedient if it is off the lead.
The
route
(please click the link in red to see it and note that if the autumn has been very wet, much of the route will be switched to tarmac lanes):
Setting off in a southerly then southeasterly direction we'll take the Downs Link former railway line and cycle path to Southwater and eventually to West Grinstead Station. Heading southwest along Park Lane we'll reach West Grinstead hamlet where we'll cross the River Adur and then, heading east, the A24. Routes through the Knepp Estate will enable us to pick up a bridleway will take us north past Green Street to the lane to Dragon's Green. A route west than northwest, then north along a lane will head back past Netherwood and Lawson's Farm to the cycle path which will return us, via the outward-bound route, back to the station.

Title: 1066 Country: East we'll Ease through Woods and Weald
Summary:
We’ll start in the mellow gold light and bonfire-scented air of a mid-October morning. We'll join the 1066 Country Walk trail through gentle fields and the Great Wood, a sprawling remnant of the ancient Wealden forest. We'll see towering oak and sweet chestnut standing in a blaze of copper and amber, their leaves carpeting the paths. We'll imagine the historical upheaval that was the Battle of Hastings, almost 960 years ago to the day. We'll admire a little of Battle Abbey, founded by King William in 1070 to celebrate his victory (and perhaps atone for his savagery). We'll take lunch and a pint in the village of Westfield and perhaps further refreshment back in Battle at the end.
The sights:
Battle Abbey:
Founded by William I in 1070 to give thanks for his victory. Remodelled in the C13. Standing in partial ruin, its gatehouse intact and dominating the town centre. Cloister arches, monastic remains, and views over the slope where Harold’s army fell bring the Conquest vividly to mind. It was destroyed in 1538 by a tyrannical beneficiary of the central, powerful English state that William created: Henry VIII. The abbey is managed by English Heritage and costs £17 to enter, so we won't be doing that.
The Battle of Hastings:
This paroxysm will have occurred almost 960 years ago on the day of the walk, when on 14 October 1066, William, Duke of Normandy, defeated King Harold II in a brutal clash that lasted most of the day and led to the loss of 6000 lives. Whether Harold's army had walked 250 miles from Stamford Bridge near York over 12 days, or whether they had sailed down the east coast, the Saxon army fought with astonishing resolve. Fighting with spears, swords and axes, they advantageously held the high ground and held the Normans off behind a shield wall. The tide turned when Harold momentarily lost control of his army when, sensing victory at the misapprehension that the Duke of Normandy was dead, they surged down the hill, abandoning the high ground and their shield wall. The Duke threw back his helmet to show that he still lived, his army rallied, and their archers and cavalry - the latter not encountered by Saxon armies before - massacred them. Legend says that Harold fell with an arrow in the eye, a fate depicted on the Bayeux Tapestry. Legend also says that his body was so vengefully mutilated that only his wife, Edith Swan-Neck, could identify it by way of secret marks on it known only to her. The consequences of the defeat were far-reaching: Norman overlords replaced local Anglo-Saxon rulers; feudalism and hierarchy were introduced; governance, culture, architecture and justice were reshaped; nascent women's rights were overturned; and England was orientated away from Scandinavia in the direction of the European core.
Westfield:
A village with its roots in the Domesday Book but not much else of historical interest. St John’s Church, rebuilt in 1815 on medieval foundations, stands at the heart of the village, its churchyard flanked by venerable yews. We will pause here for lunch and a pint at the New Inn.
The
route
(click the link to see the route)
:
We'll head down Station Approach to Lower Lake, then head northwest along Upper Lake into the town of Battle. A short excursion down Park Lane will allow us to see a little of the battlefield and abbey without having to pay £17. Returning to the High Street, we'll walk northwest up to Mount Lane before turning off and following a footpath past Little Park Farm to Marley Lane. Footpaths will take us northeast to Sedlescombe, then, having crossed the B2244, further footpaths will take us to east to Cottage Lane which will take us into Westfield for lunch at the church and a pint. We will then veer west and follow the 1066 Country Walk all the way back to Battle and the railway station.
Dogs:
I love having dogs on the walks I lead and this should be a great dog walk with woods and fields for them to run free, although the latter may contain livestock, and there will also be some country lanes and pavements. A dog off the lead must be obedient.

Title: Quiet Cotswolds: Tysoe, Epwell & Winderton
Summary:
The Cotswolds are justifiably protected as one of England's
Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty
. But that label brings with it a huge volume of visitors - especially to places like
Stow-on-the-Wold
,
Bourton-on-the-Water
and
Chipping Campden
.
Fortunately, there's a quieter side to the Cotswolds which has the same beautiful landscape but far fewer tourists. This two-county walk will explore some of those hidden gems!
Starting from
Middle Tysoe
, we head across the fields and soon face a sharp climb up
Old Lodge Hill
into a beautiful wooded area. As we emerge from the trees, we cross over the border from Warwickshire into Oxfordshire.
At
Shenington
, we join a stretch of the
Macmillan Way
- a long-distance route devised to raise funds for Macmillan Cancer Support - which runs from Lincolnshire all the way down to Dorset. We'll walk through some classic Cotswold scenery as we head down to the charming village of
Epwell
and our lunch stop.
Suitably refreshed, we’ll cross back over the border into Warwickshire and enjoy some spectacular views on the approach to the small village of
Winderton
with its prominent hilltop Victorian church.
The final leg of our walk gives a distant view of
Compton Wynyates
- a Grade I listed Tudor country house which is still in private ownership, undisturbed (and inaccessible) by visitors.
Another sharp climb takes us up to the highlight of our walk -
Tysoe Windmill
and stunning views across the surrounding countryside. Built in the early 18th century, the mill operated until 1915 when it was struck by lightning! Today, it sports a magnificent set of recently restored sails.
Dogs are welcome:
There are some short stretches on country roads and village streets. We may encounter sheep, lambs, cows or horses and there are a few fields where landowner signs request dogs on a lead.

Title: Laying bare the past in Haslingden Grane
Summary:
Our
7 miles (10.9KM)
walk explores the Grane Valley, once home to over 1000 people and part of the Forest of Rossendale, a medieval hunting forest until 1587.
Many settlements and houses have long since vanished, but we will encounter many derelict remains of homes that originally populated the area in the 16th century.
Calf Hey Reservoir, built in the 1850s robbed struggling communities of the best land for farming and the final straw was in the 1880's, with drastic falls in commodity prices.
People abandoned their homes in the poorer uplands across the region, but the depopulation of the Grane Valley is one of the most stark instances, and the upland area we will explore as a part of todays walk.
Our highest point will be Hog Low Pike at 383m, providing panoramic views across the Ribble and Bowland Valleys, Pendle Hill and the Yorkshire Dales beyond.
We will have the option of a well earned drink at the Grey Mare pub after the walk.
The rough upland footpaths and open moorland mean that sturdy boots are really an essential for this walk and being steady underfoot across open moorland and on rough paths.

Title: ODL goes to Canada and Respects to a British Icon
Summary:
In a first for OutdoorLads, we're going to Canada! But worry not! No expensive flights, no jet lag and no passports needed, as this Canada is a little hamlet in the New Forest!
Our
route
takes us straight out on to Canada Common, where the Forest's iconic ponies, donkeys and cattle roam free. After crossing the A36, we'll pass along the streets of West Wellow and then on to quiet lanes and footpaths to the smaller neighbouring hamlet of East Wellow.
Here we will find St Margaret's Church which is the final resting place of Florence Nightingale. The church itself dates back to 1215 and has many interesting wall paintings inside depicting figures such as St Christopher, Thomas Becket and St Margaret of Antioch after whom the church is named.
Florence Nightingale is generally regarded to be the founder of modern nursing, putting an emphasis on compassion, commitment to patient care and diligent and thoughtful hospital administration that had not previously been seen. She came to prominence during the Crimean War in the 1850s, and earned the nickname "The Lady with the Lamp" due to her routine of making ward rounds of the wounded soldiers at night.
With such a legacy, an offer was made for her to be buried at Westminster Abbey, but her family declined, chosing instead for her to be buried in the family plot alongside her parents. The family lived at nearby Embley Park. While the tombstone itself is reasonably large, there is no grand memorial, simply bearing her initials and birth and death dates.
With respects duly paid, we'll move on through a mix of lanes and paths following the River Blackwater upstream. After crossing back over the A36, we'll take a break at the lovely Cuckoo Inn in Hamptworth.
Our route on from there will pass through the hamlet of Nomansland with its pretty village green, through some mature oak woodland and then back on to the open spaces of Canada Common where we started.
Dogs
well-behaved dogs are welcome on the walk, but must be under close control at all times and on a lead in the vicinity of livestock or where wildlife may be disturbed. Hot weather may also make it inappropriate to bring a dog for such a distance during the middle of the day.

Title: Classic Langdale Valley Weekend
Summary:
Join OutdoorLads for a brilliant weekend in the heart of the Lake District in the Langdale Valley!
This is a classic OutdoorLads bunkhouse event—expect a friendly, social vibe, shared rooms, and a fantastic weekend of experiences in the heart of the Langdale Valley.
The Weekend & Activities
We’ll be taking full advantage of the incredible scenery right on our doorstep. On Saturday, we'll head out for a decent, proper hike up one of the nearby hills. Expect some steep inclines and challenging terrain, so please ensure you are prepared with suitable boots, warm layers, and full waterproofs!
On Saturday evening, following dinner, there are some excellent pubs on our doorstep you may choose to frequent, or you may choose stay in and play some boardgames or chill at the Bunkhouse.
What’s Included & Catering
Friday Night:
Kick off the weekend with a communal buffet as everyone arrives and settles in.
Breakfasts:
Basic continental breakfast provided on Saturday and Sunday morning to get you fuelled up.
Saturday Night:
A hearty, home-cooked group meal to refuel after a day on the hills.
Lunches:
Please bring your own food for lunches.
Key Details
Departure:
We need to be packed up, cleaned, and out of the accommodation by 11:00 AM on Sunday.
Accommodation:
Shared bunkrooms. Bedding is not provided, just a pillow. You need to bring a pillowcase, and a sleeping bag (or duvet and sheet.)
Dogs:
Unfortunately, dogs are not permitted at this venue.
Photos
: Taken by members of OutdoorLads and permission given for their use.
Difficulty & Distance: Likely to involve a decent hike with some reasonable inclines (as we are starting at the base of the valley floor!)

Title: A Literary Loop around Haworth Moor
Summary:
This scenic 8‑mile circular walk begins in
Haworth
, the historic moorland village famed for its steep cobbled Main Street and its deep connection to the Brontë family. With the Parsonage Museum nearby and sweeping views toward the Pennines, Haworth provides an evocative starting point for a day immersed in Yorkshire’s literary landscape.
Leaving the village, the route heads out toward
Penistone Hill Country Park
, a broad expanse of former quarry land now reclaimed by heather, grasses, and wildlife. Its rolling terrain and wide horizons offer early panoramic views across the moors, setting the tone for the rugged scenery ahead.
From Penistone Hill, the path continues westward toward the quiet valley of South Dean Beck, arriving at
Brontë Bridge
, a picturesque stone crossing set in a sheltered hollow. The sound of the beck and the surrounding moorland create a timeless atmosphere, echoing the landscapes that inspired the Brontë sisters.
Beyond the bridge, the route climbs steadily onto the high moor, following well‑trodden tracks toward
Top Withins
. The ruined farmhouse sits isolated on the ridge, long associated romantically if not literally with the Earnshaw home in
Wuthering Heights
. The approach is dramatic, with sweeping views and the unmistakable sense of wildness that defines this part of the Pennines.
The return leg descends from Top Withins toward the moorland village of
Stanbury
, offering a change of scenery as the rugged heights give way to lanes, cottages, and valley views. Here we can enjoy a well‑earned refreshment stop at the
Wuthering Heights pub
, a welcoming spot with views across the surrounding hills.
The final stretch follows paths and tracks that gradually lead back towards Haworth and brings us once again into the village.

Title: Boxing Day Calorie Burner
Summary:
Whether you’re looking to walk off a few Christmas calories or simply fancy stretching your legs over the holiday, I hope you’ll join me for an
8‑mile (12.8km)
Boxing Day walk across the varied landscapes of
Cannock Chase
.
Cannock Chase, designated an
Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty
in 1958, is the smallest AONB in mainland Britain at around
26 square miles
. Its mix of woodland, heathland and open valleys makes it a perfect place for a refreshing winter walk.
Our route will explore both well‑known and lesser‑visited parts of the Chase, including
The Old Acre Valley
,
The Glacier Boulder
,
Anson’s Bank
, and the
Katyn Memorial
. We’ll return via stretches of the
Heart of England Way
and the peaceful
Sher Brook Valley
, with opportunities for sweeping views across northern and eastern Staffordshire.
The Chase is home to a herd of around
800+ fallow deer
, so keep your eyes peeled for wildlife along the way.

Title: Coombe Country Park Circular
Summary:
Join Samuel for a 7 mile/11.2km circular walk from Coombe Abbey Country Park. In 1771 the 6th Baron Craven commissioned Capability Brown to modernise the landscape around the former Cistercian monastery at Coombe Abbey. Brown swept away the elaborate Elizabethan gardens and landscaped the park to create a serpentine lake, sweeping views and extensive new planting.
We will start by weaving through the wooded paths of the park before exiting onto bridle paths and country roads, skirting Birchley Wood before returning to Coombe Abbey via the Twelve O'clock ride.
Due to the nature of the ground. I recommend walking boots or shoes for this walk due to the uneven ground in parts.
Well behaved dogs are welcome on this walk.

Title: The Enchanted Forest Light Show
Summary:
By day, Faskally Forest near Pitlochry is a beautiful array of mixed woodland with some very tall trees indeed. It has lochans and a network of paths to entice you into the forest's depths.
For about 4 weeks a year, as the sun gets low in the sky, and when we put the clocks back, the forest is transformed by a mesmerising and interactive light show that blows your mind, "How have they come up with that?" It's not just about lights, it's about how they (a) mesmerise and (b) with narration educate about the importance of life in our forests for just about every other form of life on the planet.
WHEN?
OutdoorLads will be going on Sunday 1st November, 5.30pm. We're likely to be inside the forest for up to two hours. Clocks go back before then, sunset will be 4.30, so properly dark by 5.30.
WHAT'S THE PLAN?
Most importantly,
YOU HAVE TO PURCHASE YOUR OWN ENTRANCE TICKET
Signing up to the event page alone does not get you in. The ticket prices are about £40 but there are some concessions available.
Buy your ticket for Sunday 1st November, 17.30 slot. If this fills, you could buy for the slots either side and meet the rest of us inside.
The ticket includes coach travel from the centre of Pitlochry (close to the railway station) - you cannot gain access in your own vehicle. It includes the return of course.
WHAT ELSE MIGHT WE DO ON THE DAY?

If you're travelling by public transport, Pitlochry is well connected by rail and coach services with Ember, Citylink and Flixbus. Check engineering works that might affect Sunday and especially late Sunday trains.

Title: High Peak ‘in-steam’ Heritage Day Walk
Summary:
We will meet at Cromford Wharf Carpark, a short walk from Cromford Railway Station at 10.30am. I’ll be arriving at Cromford Mill, over the road from the carpark an hour beforehand so if you get in earlier they’ll be a chance to join me for a short tour.
A challenging walk taking in beautiful scenery, an abundance of wildlife, cracking views, and world renowned heritage, the Derwent Valley Mills having been awarded World Heritage Status in 2001. Cromford Canal is a haven for wildlife and a Site of Special Scientific Interest with little grebes and water voles, dragonflies, damselflies and hoverflies.
From Cromford Mill where there are a number of interesting buildings, we will follow the towpath from Cromford Wharf for one and a quarter miles to Leawood Pumping House.  The Pumping House was built in 1849 to pump water from the River Derwent into the canal, it operated for almost 100 years.
The walk has been planned to coincide with Heritage Open Days 2026 and a steaming day of two beam engines - Leawood Pumping Station and Middleton Top Engine House.
Experience the power of steam, the heat of the boilers, the smell of grease and coal and the power of the wave as tons of water are pumped...
Following this we will cross the canal walking between the old railway buildings of the High Peak Junction to ascend the steep High Peak Trail. At the foot of the incline is a catch pit, where runaway wagons once came to rest. On reaching the summit and Engine House we will be rewarded with views over the Derwent Valley. Remaining on the High Peak Trail we will aim to lunch at Black Rocks Visitor Centre (drinks and home-made cakes available here). Then onto Middleton Top where we will leave the Trail and walk though the historic limestone village of Middleton-by-Wirksworth before descending to meet the Via Gellia road and then onto Water Lane and Scarthin with views over Cromford Dam.
Those of you who would like to stay on might enjoy Arkwright’s Mill, Cromford village and/or a village pub to enjoy a well-earned pint or two before heading home.

Title: Sheffield bouldering @ Depot Climbing
Summary:
Swap trainers for climbing shoes and join OutdoorLads for an evening of INDOOR BOULDERING at Depot Climbing in Sheffield.
If you’re new to Depot Climbing it’s one of the biggest bouldering centres in Sheffield with plenty of challenging routes that will give you the PUMP your arms crave.
Cards/contactless ONLY  - this venue does not accept cash
If you haven't been to Depot Climbing before, please click
here

climbing
faster.

.
What is Bouldering?
It's a form of climbing where instead of long high routes, the 'problems' tend to be shorter and focus on technique, balance, body positioning and sometimes power. Because of this different emphasis, bouldering doesn't have the hassle of climbing with ropes, harnesses and belaying, which makes it an excellent activity for newcomers to the sport. No wonder it's often regarded as the 'purest' form of climbing.
If you're a seasoned climber you won't need convincing about the benefits of bouldering, but for those who've never climbed more than a staircase, the benefits are wide ranging: from the physical - improved strength, tone, balance, power and coordination; mental - problem solving, focus, concentration and body awareness; to the emotional - relaxation, a sense of achievement and a feeling that mind and body are working together perfectly ('feeling psyched'). On top of all this, bouldering tends to be a very social sport where you can hang out with mates and each have a go as you feel regardless of what level you climb at.
I'm new to Bouldering - can I come along?
If you have never tried bouldering before it is recommended that you have a guided session from the event leader, who will go through everything you will need to know to boulder safely before joining in with the rest of the group.
I've been Bouldering before?
As above, everyone attending the event  must abide by the centre's T&Cs etc. As an experienced boulderer you responsible for your own safety, actions and involvement at all times. As such, you should use your own judgement in taking up advice given either by OutdoorLads Volunteers or other experienced climbers.
Photos : Copyright granted to OutdoorLads by the event leader / venue.
Please note that every person participating should be aware of (and accept) that those members perceived as ‘in charge’ or leading the event are not necessarily qualified, do not need to be qualified, and are not regarded by OutdoorLads, or themselves as ‘technical experts’ but are amateur climbers with some experience and who are happy to impart their knowledge. Any advice given should be considered with this in mind by the recipient.
All those attending the event must also be aware of the centre's own terms and conditions of participation and abide by them, along with any instructions given by the centre’s staff. Everyone must also take responsibility for their own safety while participating in Indoor climbing events.

We’ll set off from within the park and make our way around, visiting the folly built in the late 18th century as a summerhouse. We’ll take our time, enjoy the scenery, and make the most of the park. There will be three opportunities for refreshments during the walk, so there’s no need to bring food, although you’re very welcome to do so.

Title: Bannau Brycheiniog Autumn Escape: The Brecon Peaks
Summary:
Join us for a fantastic autumn weekend away in the heart of the
Bannau Brycheiniog (Brecon Beacons)
We’ll be staying at a beautiful converted farmhouse surrounded by wooded slopes, rushing rivers, and dramatic peaks.
Whether you’re looking to conquer some serious mountain summits or enjoy a scenic, relaxed stroll along historic waterways, this weekend has something for everyone.
The hostel is a charmingly converted traditional Welsh farmhouse steeped in rustic character. It perfectly balances a remote, "getaway" vibe with modern comfort.
Historic Character:
The hostel retains its gorgeous original stonework, exposed timber beams, and a cozy lounge complete with a
wood-burning stove
—the ultimate spot to swap stories and unwind with the guys after a day on the trails.
Stunning Natural Setting:
Tucked away in a secluded valley just below the
Talybont Reservoir
, the hostel is surrounded by lush wooded slopes, cascading waterfalls, and rushing streams. You literally step out of the front door and directly onto the trails.
Dark Skies Oasis:
The area surrounding the hostel is a designated
International Dark Sky Reserve
. If the night is clear, you can take a five-minute stroll to the edge of the reservoir for breathtaking, unpolluted views of the constellations and the moon reflecting on the water.
The Weekend Plan
Friday: The Social Kick-off
Arrive from 4:30 PM and settle into our mountain home. We’ll kick things off with our traditional welcome buffet—a great chance to meet everyone and plot our adventures.
Note: Please bring a small contribution to share (enough for 2-3 people). Let’s keep it varied—creative salads, local meats, or snacks are great, but maybe let’s go easy on the quiche!
Saturday: The Main Event
We have two brilliant options for Saturday's walk, which will be finalised closer to the date depending on weather and group preference:
Option A: The Mountain High
– A classic, invigorating hike into the nearby Brecon Beacons peaks. Expect breathtaking ridges, stunning vistas, and a good workout.
Option B: The Canal Circuit
– A gentler but incredibly scenic circular walk tracking the historic Monmouthshire & Brecon Canal between Llangynidr and Talybont-on-Usk. Perfect for autumn colors, locks, and easy-going socializing.
Sunday: Morning Stretch & Depart
After breakfast, we'll pack up and check out. For those not rushing off, we can head out for a short local stroll or a pub lunch nearby before saying our goodbyes.
Food & Fuel
We’ve got you covered so you can focus on the views:
Included:
Breakfasts on Saturday and Sunday, plus a delicious group dinner on Saturday night.
Tea, Coffee & Cake:
Plenty provided throughout the weekend—because every hiker needs a sugar hit!
Your Part:

Title: Family Christmas in the Yorkshire Dales
Summary:
A Christmas of memories with your OutdoorLads family.
We wish you a Family Christmas, we wish you a Family Christmas…
so come spend it with us in the Yorkshire Dales.
Family Christmas returns to Yorkshire, in one of the most welcoming spots we know! Join Chris and Mike for a festive three-nights in the Yorkshire Dales.
Whether you’re looking for a change from your usual plans or simply want somewhere to belong this year, we’ll be here to cook for you, laugh with you, and keep the festive spirit flowing. Expect chilled evenings in the lounge, maybe a movie night, a cheeky dance, terrible cracker jokes, and plenty of food.
With the Dales right outside the door, we’ll stretch our legs on Christmas Day and take a longer walk on Boxing Day, though you’re just as welcome to stay cosy inside with board games, chats, or a well‑earned nap.
Cheesy jumpers encouraged, Secret Santa guaranteed.
It’s the perfect way to spend the season — together, relaxed, and surrounded by the beauty of the Dales.
Accommodation
Our venue is a spacious independent hostel with a good size lounge and separate dining room, cosy conservatory area and a large kitchen together with bike store and a range of bedroom sizes. Outside, there's a large garden with beautiful views in every direction. If the weather is good there's a firepit, and a chance to relax around a fire. If not don't worry, we have the cosy hostel for comfort, relaxing chatting, board games etc.
There is no TV and while there is WiFi it can be patchy, so this hostel is a chance to socialise away from our screens!
There's a small but well stocked village shop a short walk away and provides all you may need, and there's a choice of excellent pubs in the village serving home cooked food (depending upon their Christmas opening times).
Food

Title: Dolgellau Double 2: The Precipice Walk
Summary:
Route Description
The 4 mile Dolgellau Precipice Walk, as it is known locally, runs around the 12th Century Nannau estate and along the shore of Llyn Cynwch a working reservoir that provides Dolgellau with water. The path will take you through woodlands and meadows and then along a trail that clings to the edge of the hill (hence the name). Don't worry it isn't that scary! There are  captivating views of Yr Wddfa and the Moelwynion to the north, The Rhinogydd to the west, whilst Cader Idris, the Aran and Arenig ranges can be seen towards the south and east.
Although the path stands at 800ft above sea level, the starting point is already high up, so the route is relatively flat, and the reward factor vs effort expended is great. The route makes a good introduction to the area and is perfect to follow the more energetic route the day before. (see below)
After the circular route there is a hillfort on an adjacent hill to explore taking an hour or so. This part is 2 miles with 200m of height gain.  Those who prefer otherwise could be on their way home, or return to the town for tea and cake etc.

https://www.outdoorlads.com/events/dolgellau-double-1-beautiful-afon-mawddach-260912
.

Title: Dolgellau Double 1: The beautiful Afon Mawddach
Summary:
Route Description
Our walk starts and ends in the charming and historic market town of Dolgellau (pronounced like Dol-geth-lie) which started life in the Welsh gold rush times, was famous for ship building and is now popular with hikers and climbers exploring the Cadair Idris mountain range that looms over the town. Our walk explores the land above the upper reaches of the stunning Mawddach Estuary.
Initially we will take a back lane out of the town to the small settlement of Llaneltyd where it joins with the Arfon Mawddach. We then ascend sharply up the side of Foel Ipris (328 m) to a level section on the hillside from where in good weather we will get some beautiful views down the estuary towards the coast, and of the Cadir Idris mountain range.
We descend back down through the forest and cross the river on a rustic and historic wooden toll bridge (charge
30 pence
–
please bring change
), to stop for a drink on the incredibly scenic terraces of the George III Hotel in Penmaenpool: Wales 'pub of the year'.
The last sector of the walk follows a disused railway which is now a well established cycle and walking route, and follows the Arfon Wnion back into the town. For those that wish to round off the day, Dolgellau has some great cafes and eateries.

Title: Fields, Woods & Wildlife: the Great Everdon Escapade
Summary:
This is a walk that may surprise anyone who is unfamiliar with this part of middle England; a beautiful 9-mile circular through the rolling hills of
South Northamptonshire
. Our walk takes in a selection of charming villages packed full of ironstone cottages, plenty of rural views, an enchanting wood and a stately home which now serves as a luxury country house hotel.
Starting on the village green in
Everdon
, we'll take the No Through Road up to the hamlet of
Little Everdon
, before cutting across the fields to
Newnham
. From there, we pick up the first mile or so of the
Nene Way
– a 110 mile path which starts in Northamptonshire and runs through Cambridgeshire and Lincolnshire all the way up to The Wash.
After skirting around
Badby
, we join the start of the
Knightley Way
– a scenic path that runs down to Towcester. One of the highlights of the walk takes us around the edge of Badby Wood – a
Site of Special Scientific Interest
and a haven for wildlife which has a history of continuous woodland cover for over seven hundred years.
Emerging from the wood, we cross over Badby Down to enjoy the first of a series of spectacular viewing spots where you can gaze at miles of unspoilt English countryside. We'll pause here for our picnic lunch, overlooking
Fawsley Hall
– a Grade I listed country hotel and spa.
Descending down past Fawsley and its tiny church which sits perched on a grassy knoll surrounded by a ha-ha to keep the cattle out, we cross the fields again and head up to the village of
Preston Capes
.
Here the gently undulating terrain becomes a little bit more challenging; after climbing up to Preston Capes and descending back down to the east of the village, we're in for a surprisingly steep climb back up to the corner of Mantles Heath. But the climb is well worth it – we're rewarded with more spectacular views looking northwards towards Daventry and Warwickshire beyond.
Having caught our breath, it's back down into the valley and across the fields to return to Everdon and an opportunity to quench our thirst at
The Plough Inn
.

Title: Fireside evenings above the Calder Valley
Summary:
A weekend retreat to remember!
Perched high above the Calder Valley, this 17th‑century Grade II listed camping barn has a real off‑the‑beaten‑track feel, surrounded by open countryside and wide Pennine views. It’s a perfect place to experience the autumn leaves and the breezes that sweep across the rolling hills.
From the barn, there are many options for nearby walks include the dramatic ridge to Stoodley Pike, loops around local reservoirs, or gentler valley walks towards Hebden Bridge and Hardcastle Crags. For those wanting something lower level, there are plenty of scenic paths straight from the door. If you’re not walking, you can head into Todmorden or Hebden Bridge for cafés, shops and a slower day, or settle in for a reading day in the large indoor activity space.
This event is a two‑night weekend retreat. Walks will take place on Saturday, with routes chosen closer to the time based on weather. It’s also a great opportunity to get involved in route planning if you’d like to contribute.
Accommodation
The barn is simple, but we’ll create fantastic memories through community, conversation and cosy fireside moments. This peaceful rural setting is a great way to experience the wilder side of West Yorkshire. Expect a couple of days of walking, cooking together and being part of a friendly, welcoming group.
There are three bunk‑bed rooms sleeping 8, 10 and 12 people, plus a fourth accessible room. No bedding is provided – you MUST bring your own sleeping bag, bedding and pillow.
We’ve got access to a well‑equipped kitchen with fridge/freezer, a lounge area, an accessible wet‑room shower, toilet blocks, and a large indoor barn space for activities. Wi‑Fi is available.
Heating is provided by wood‑pellet and multifuel stoves, and there’s also an outdoor fire pit and campfire area for relaxed evenings.
Food
Friday night will be a buffet – please bring something to share. Saturday night will be a shared meal cooked by the leader, with breakfast included on both Saturday and Sunday mornings.

Title: Dartmoor Circular: Forests, Tors, and Ancient Stones
Summary:
Join us for a spectacular, varied circular day hike right through the atmospheric heart of northeastern Dartmoor. This route truly has a bit of everything: rushing rivers, deep evergreen forests, exposed ridge lines, stunning panoramic tors, and some of the finest prehistoric monuments the moor has to offer.
Setting out from near the iconic Warren House Inn, we’ll start by dropping south towards the peaceful valley of Soussons Down, winding through the trees before looping west past historic farmsteads towards Postbridge. Here, we'll cross the East Dart River near its famous ancient clapper bridge.
From Postbridge, we begin our steady northward march along the edge of the open moorland, tracking beneath Hartland Tor and Stannon Tor, with wide-open views expanding out to the west. We'll climb up towards Grey Wethers—the striking twin bronze-age stone circles nestled right on the edge of the woods.
Our route then takes a scenic, sheltered turn into the pine-scented tracks of Fernworthy Forest, skirting the southern edge of the beautiful Fernworthy Reservoir. After a quick stop to admire the water and the nearby hut circles, we’ll break back out onto the open moor via Chagford Common and Hurston Ridge. Our final stretch carries us south along the ridge line, enjoying commanding views of the landscape before returning to Warren House Inn for a well-earned drink.
Dogs
Dogs are welcome to join us on this event but we do ask the following:
Please appreciate the fact that not everyone is a dog owner or lover- especially when we stop to eat
Please ensure you adhere to the Countryside Code at all times - see (
Keeping Dogs Under Effective Control)
If your dog is uncontrolled and strays in open land frightening other animals or livestock, the leader is supported by the OutdoorLads board of trustees to ask you to leave the event as this is not acceptable behaviour.

Title: Icknield Way: Pegsdon Hills
Summary:
Join Alex for this slightly longer 14-mile Chiltern circular walk via the Icknield Way.
We will begin in the Hertfordshire town of Hitchin and our route will take us south out of the the town centre. Here we will turn west and follow the Chiltern Way into undulating countryside and ascend the beginnings of the Chiltern escarpment as we approach the village of Great Offley, named after the Mercian King Offa. After leaving the village we will turn north, passing the the 12th-century church of Mary Magdalene, and head out into open fields for another couple of miles.
Shortly after crossing into Bedfordshire we will reach the Pegsdon Hills, with wide-ranging views to the north. We may see some Highland cattle grazing as we join the the Icknield Way and follow it the along ridge of the hills towards the trig point at Deacon Hill. Our route will descend sharply before we head into woodland, passing by the edge of the Knocking Hoe nature reserve which also has good views of the surrounding farmland and villages.
Continuing on the Icknield Way we will head east towards the pleasant village of Pirton where the parish church of St Mary sits beside the remaining earthworks of a castle. From here we will walk back towards Hitchin, entering the town via the Oughtonhead nature reserve with its herd of English longhorn cattle. We will pass through the town centre, via Market Place and another St Mary's church, before heading back towards the station.

Title: Halloween at Dunster: Castles, Coast, and Celtic Hills
Summary:
Join us for a fantastic, varied Halloween day walk exploring the dramatic landscapes surrounding the historic medieval village of Dunster. This is a relatively short, circular route packed with diverse scenery—taking us from ancient wooded hills and historic settlements to the sweeping Somerset coastline, before tracking the nostalgic West Somerset Railway.
We’ll finish with plenty of time to spare in the afternoon to explore the magnificent Dunster Castle and its gorgeous gardens. Costumes are entirely optional, but a bit of Halloween spirit is highly encouraged!
Event Overview
Date:
Saturday, 31st October 2026
Duration:
Approximately 4 hours (excluding castle visit)
Distance:
Around 8.5 miles (13.5 km)
Difficulty:
Moderate. A few steady climbs into the hills, but well-paced with plenty of flat coastal walking to balance it out.
The Route
We begin our journey in the shadow of Dunster Castle, heading straight out into the atmospheric autumnal canopy of Dunster Park.
The Highs:
We’ll climb steadily up through the woods towards the ancient iron-age hillforts of
Bat’s Castle
and
Black Ball
, offering spectacular, moody views over the surrounding Somerset landscape and the Bristol Channel.
The Valleys & Villages:
Skirting the ridges of Aller Hill and Withycombe Hill, we'll drop down through the quiet combes and charming villages of Withycombe and Carhampton.
The Coast:
From Carhampton, we head north to meet the coast at
Blue Anchor
. Here, we'll grab some fresh sea air and look out across the waves.
The Rails:
The final leg brings us back west, tracking alongside the historic
West Somerset Railway
line and crossing the flat marshlands straight back into Dunster.
Afternoon: Dunster Castle & Gardens
After wrapping up the walk, the afternoon is yours to enjoy. We will head over to Dunster Castle (managed by the National Trust). Perched dramatically on a tor, this ancient fortress turned grand country house is the perfect setting for a Halloween afternoon.
You can wander through the multi-tiered subtropical gardens, explore the historic mill, or head inside the castle to soak up centuries of history (and perhaps a ghost story or two).
> Note: National Trust members get into the castle and gardens for free, so remember to bring your membership card! Non-members can purchase tickets on the day.
A Few Haunted Highlights... 🕷️
Dunster has a reputation for being one of the most active paranormal hotspots in the country—local lore says nearly every historic building in the village has a resident spirit. The castle itself has been investigated by the National Trust for its eerie occurrences. Keep an eye out for:
The Grey Lady:
Dunster’s most famous resident spectre, she is frequently seen gliding majestically down the grand 17th-century oak staircase before completely vanishing into a solid wall.
The Man in Green:
If you pop into the National Trust gift shop (housed in the old 17th-century stable block), you might spot a mysterious figure dressed head-to-toe in green walking calmly through the building before disappearing into thin air.
The Chinking of Coins:
On certain days, the ghostly sound of money being counted echoes near the old keeps. Local legend attributes this to the infamous William de Mohun ("The Scourge of the West"), who minted his own illegal currency here during the medieval Civil War.
The Foot of the Blue Kitchen:
In one of the modernised volunteer areas known as the Blue Kitchen, a shaken worker once reported a completely disembodied, naked human foot appearing out of nowhere on the floor before dissolving.
The Seven-Foot Skeleton:
Deep beneath the Gatehouse dungeon, archaeologists once uncovered the remains of a prisoner standing over seven feet tall, still shackled by his wrists and ankles to the stone wall. While no specific ghost has been spotted, visitors note a distinct drop in temperature, and dogs notoriously refuse to go near the steps leading down to it.
Even on our walk before we reach the castle, keep your ears open—tourists on the nearby hills have previously reported the distinct, booming sound of a massive troop of soldiers marching past them, despite the hillsides being completely empty!
If you want to get a little extra Spooky, Dunster Castle is running Ghost Tours after dark when the castle is closed to the public on Halloween.  It's £25 a ticket and I've booked myself onto the 7pm tour.  If you want to join me, you can book a ticket here:
https://www.nationaltrust-tickets.org.uk/event-tickets/34525?
What to Bring
Footwear:
Sturdy walking boots or muddy-trail shoes are highly recommended, as the woodland and hill paths can be damp and slick in late October.
Clothing:
Layer up for autumn weather and bring a reliable waterproof jacket—the coastal stretch can get breezy!
Food & Drink:
Pack a packed lunch, snacks, and plenty of water for the trail. We will find a scenic spot along the hills or coast for a lunch stop.
Money/Card:
For entry to the Castle/Gardens if you aren't an NT member, or for a well-deserved hot drink/pint in Dunster afterwards.
Dogs
Dogs are welcome to join us on this event but we do ask the following:
Please appreciate the fact that not everyone is a dog owner or lover- especially when we stop to eat
Please ensure you adhere to the Countryside Code at all times - see (
Keeping Dogs Under Effective Control)
If your dog is uncontrolled and strays in open land frightening other animals or livestock, the leader is supported by the OutdoorLads board of trustees to ask you to leave the event as this is not acceptable behaviour.

Title: Yorkshire Three Peaks Hostel 2026
Summary:
Join OutdoorLads for an early September hostel break to walk the
Yorkshire Three Peaks!
You've probably heard of the National Three Peaks of Ben Nevis, Snowdon/Yr Wyddfa and Scafell Pike, in many ways more a driving challenge than a walking challenge, and requiring a certain level of insomnia.
But did you know there is also a famous walking challenge in Yorkshire too, walking (approximately) a marathon
over a circuit of Whernside, Ingleborough and Pen y Ghent in the Dales?  It's that challenge we will be undertaking on this hostel weekend, with the added benefit of a comfortable lounge to sit in and a proper (bunk) bed to sleep in afterwards!
Why not do some other OutdoorLads mountain walks to get your fitness up before tackling the challenge?
Don't worry, though, if it turns out you can't make it all the way round, the route takes us past Horton-in-Ribblesdale station where it would be possible to take a train back to Ribblehead, and it'd be possible to bail off after our first mountain, Whernside, and head for the pub.  So if you think you can do it and fancy a go please do sign up!
The Plan
Friday evening
: arrive from 4:30pm (no earlier please), we will have the traditional OutdoorLads buffet and a briefing around 8pm before socialising at the hostel or maybe a visit to the local pub.
Saturday
: we will be up quite early to head out after breakfast onto the main event, the Yorkshire Three Peaks walk, with the aim being to complete it within 12 hours if possible.  When we get back we'll have tea/coffee and cake, and a hearty dinner which I'm sure we will all need by then, then we can socialise in the hostel, pop out to the pub or if you're really worn out maybe an early night - or perhaps bring your favourite board game if that's your thing?
Sunday
: after breakfast it'll be time to pack, sort out the hostel and say our goodbyes.  I don't plan as things stand to offer a Sunday walk (we'll all be tired!) but you might want to do some touristing around the local area before heading home?
Sponsorship?
Unlike the Keswick to Barrow walk which OutdoorLads also takes part in as a fundraiser, this isn't specifically being run as a sponsored event, but if you fancy doing some fundraising yourself as part of this walk, either for OutdoorLads or for another charity of your choice, please feel free (and thanks in advance if you do decide to support OutdoorLads!)
Other Activities
While the main intention of this hostel is to complete the Three Peaks of Yorkshire walk, if other mountain or lowland leaders join the event it may be possible to offer shorter walks as well.  If you are such a leader, please send me a message via my profile below to let me know what you are interested in offering and I will note it on here.  Thank you :)
It would also be possible to stay with us in the hostel and do your own thing if you're a cyclist or just want to "train geek out" and have a ride on the scenic Settle-Carlisle Line (the town of Settle is said to be a nice day out, as is the city of Carlisle), take some photos of the famous Ribblehead Viaduct, have a meal and a pint at the Station Inn or just chill at the hostel!  If this is your intention please send me a message when you've booked on so I know I don't need to account for you on the main walk.
Dogs
Regrettably this event is not suitable for dogs - the walk is probably too long for most and they are not allowed in the hostel by the owners.  Sorry!

Title: Hereford and Breinton Springs
Summary:
Join Alex for a slow and largely flat 10km / 6 mile walk from Hereford Cathedral to the National Trust site of
Breinton Springs
.
This short walk starts and finishes in the cathedral grounds in Hereford and takes a leisurely stroll along the river Wye.
Along the way you get some stunning views of the cathedral and the river before ending up in a peaceful churchyard surrounded by ancient orchards and the possibility of coming face to face with some endangered wildlife in an SSSI. We also walk past the spot where a dog fell into the Wye more than a hundred years ago, inspiring Elgar to write one of the
Enigma Variations
. On our return to the city we take a loop through the site where
Hereford Castle
once stood.
The walk is planned for the end of September, so if you wished to stay in Hereford until the following day, you could join the
Queers & Beers monthly meet up
, which normally takes place on the last Sunday of the month. And if you were to arrive early, you could pop to the café in All Saints Church to check out a
particularly rude wood carving
.
If this is your first ODL event, you should check out the information designed specifically for you on the
My First Event
page on the ODL website.
Note:
If there are no places left on this event, join the waiting list, as people frequently drop out during the week before an event, and you are likely to get a place.

Title: Northern Ireland's Causeway Coast
Summary:
We're off over the Irish Sea for four nights to explore the Causeway Coast.
Our hostel has a sea view and is in an ideal location for seeing the various attractions of the area - top of the list is the Causeway Coast itself with its hexagonal basalt columns, this being part of a fine coastal walk. Also within walking distance of the hostel is Carrick-a-Rede rope bridge, perhaps not for those with a fear of heights as it hangs 30m above the sea!
A short drive away is Ballycastle with the historic Bonamargy Friary and it's harbour, this being the port for the short sailing to Rathlin Island - an island six miles long with tranquil walking trails and views back across the causeway coast. If we go a little further east we find ourselves in the Glens of Antrim, an area of ancient woodlands and waterfalls with several beautiful walking trails.
There is lots more to see and do, but why not just come along and discover this stunning part of Northern Ireland....
Our hostel has lots of social space, free table tennis & pool and clean, comfortable dorm rooms - plus a pub 100m away. It's absolutely perfect as a base to explore the local area and this stunning coastline.

Title: Gran Canaria Adventure Week 2027
Summary:
The last four years have proven to be hugely successful and popular...
so we're doing all it all again in 2027!!!
Gran Canaria Adventure Week
is back again for
January 2027
. We have some of what you've loved from previous years, plus new events and ideas to give you an even better winter sun experience.
Feedback from previous years:
"The socials were well organised and the group events were excellent"
"Loved the ability to do as much or as little as we wanted throughout the entire week"
"A fantastic event with something for everyone"
"Good range of activities to keep everyone happy, from leisure city tours to high octane hikes, canyoning, via ferrata - something for everyone! And the organisers are friendly and welcoming, feels like family which is nice"
"All the event leaders were great and super friendly and easy to talk to and ask questions"
Think you know Gran Canaria? Think again!
Let your next (or first!) visit to Gran Canaria be one filled with outdoor adventures. While the island is known as a year-round party destination for LGBTQ+ visitors, this trip is an opportunity to experience something different:
take part in outdoor activities; experience the beauty of the "real" Gran Canaria; and meet friends from around the world.
We are, once again, partnering with
CanCanaria
to bring you a full week of fun and adventurous activities. CanCanaria is a gay-owned and run company based on Gran Canaria, using their extensive local knowledge and the island's magnificent natural beauty to create a programme of excursions and trips that'll leave you with unforgettable memories and stories to tell. At the helm is former OutdoorLads' Chairman Patrick, so you know you will be in good and welcoming hands. Patrick and his team use trusted local volunteers, guides and instructors who are LGBTQ+ friendly, and who hold appropriate insurance and qualifications where necessary.
The
CanCanaria Adventure Week
is festival dedicated to outdoor activities, combining adventures with a holiday in the sun and sociable evenings. Expect
Hiking, Climbing, Sailing, Surfing and Scuba Diving alongside tourist trips, socials, restaurants, bars, a pool party and boat trips.
How do I sign up?
Sign up to this OutdoorLads event
in the usual way. This doesn't get you a place on the CanCanaria event, but it will enable us to see how many of our members are attending, make arrangements together and share details and information easily in the run up to the trip.
Sign up to the CanCanaria Activity Week
on their website
by following this link
. This step is free and simply gets you a place on the overall event. It will also enable CanCanaria to contact you with details of the activities as they become available. You'll be asked to indicate the types of activities you are interested in, and the organisers will then use that information to formulate the final programme.
Sign up to whatever combination of activities and parties you fancy via the pages which CanCanaria will publish in due course
. If you've signed up at Step 2, you will also be notified as the various activities get arranged.
***VIP Offer***
CanCanaria have put together a VIP package. For a fixed price, you get:
50 euro voucher to spend on Adventure Week activities,
only for orders made before September 1st 2026
VIP Breakfast/Brunch
- only available to those with VIP Tickets (10:00 - 12:00: Wednesday 27 January)
Free Entry To:
The Welcome Party, (Monday 25 January)
The Main Pool Party, BBQ included (Wednesday 27 January)
The Sundown BBQ, men only event - BBQ included (Friday 28 January)
Office Adventure Week 2027 T-shirt
One CanCanaria Passport
- a book of discount vouchers to use in bars, shops and restaurants in Maspalomas
Those of us who have attended in previous years have had an amazing trip. There has been a great range of activities which really showed off the beauty of the island, and the evening socials (in a different bar each night) meant there was a regular opportunity to catch up with everyone, get to know your fellow travellers and ask any questions of the events team.
Check out some of the photos on this page which are from previous years!
It is entirely up to you whether you come to Gran Canaria for some or all of the week, or indeed whether you arrive earlier or leave later to make it part of a longer trip.

Gran Canaria has accommodation to suit a variety of budgets, from basic self-catering apartments, to full service hotels and villas.
You are welcome to message the event leader or Patrick at CanCanaria for accommodation ideas, and to use the event page comments to arrange sharing. In due course we will also set up an OutdoorLads Telegram group too.

Title: An Evening with the Stars in Nottinghamshire
Summary:
We have secured a booking for a group visit to
Sherwood Observatory
.
Since its recent re-opening, the Observatory has been booked solid with group tours so we are pleased to offer this opportunity in Autumn 2026.
The visit promises a 90 minute adventure you'll never forget including a chance to ask anything you want to know about space and beyond. Additionally there will be:
a 20+ minute planetarium show and presentation by the expert team
a captivating talk in the lecture room that will spark your imagination
a thrilling opportunity to gaze at the stars and planets or our closest star, the Sun, depending on the season, (weather dependent)
a tour of the radio astronomy facilities
a visit of exhibition in the Science Centre to learn more about human space flight and the history of the Reservoir
Photos: Sherwood Observatory and used with permission
Difficulty & Distance: Sit and watch the stars go by. The site is broadly accessible but visiting the main telescope involves climbing some steps

Title: BIG20: THE Celebration Event - Hostel
Summary:
Where did the 20 years go!? It's been an epic tens of thousands of miles walked, climbed, skied, kayaked, cycled; thousands of friendships made; and an immeasurable amount of laughter and incredible memories.
We hope you can join us in the Peak District to celebrate this epic milestone!
There are three accommodation types for this event, so please ensure you book on the correct one:
Hostel
(this event page)
Pods
Camping
All accommodation types include the catering and entertainment in the main building.
The hostel has a range of modern, all-ensuite rooms with bunk beds. They are spacious and well appointed, this is a lovely hostel!
The weekend will include a formal AGM which all Full/Concession Members are very much encouraged to attend to help us formally celebrate our amazing volunteers and members. (If you want to attend just the AGM and not stay at the hostel or for the party, that will be possible and details will be made available in due course, along with details of the AGM live stream.)
You can also expect amazing walks and other events offered by our volunteers, on-site activities (is that a zip wire on top of the building!?), spectacular food, a fully-stocked bar, a late night disco with DJ Dan, and we're going to party like its 2016 with a Ceilidh with Triple Scotch (yes, they want to come back!)!
Whether you have been a member since 2006 when we formed or only just joined us today - all are welcome and all have played a part creating, shaping and continuing this wonderful organisation which has changed lives, brought lifelong friends together (and even husbands!), and given everyone the chance to try something new with our wide range of activities for all.
You don't want to miss out on this epic weekend, so get booking!

support@outdoorlads.com
and we can arrange that. We'll discuss with you how much you'd like to pay each month and a time frame over which you'd like to pay. You will need to have paid in full by the 31 August.
OutdoorLads Foundation

, and hopefully we can get you celebrating with us!
